headline: Can the size of your amygdala give away your politics?
title: Political Orientations Are Correlated with Brain Structure in Young Adults
note: The researchers compared young adults’ self-reported politics with brain anatomy. They linked greater conservatism to a larger right amygdala and greater liberalism to more gray matter in the anterior cingulate cortex. Preregistered replication: in a sample of 928, the positive amygdala association was r = 0.068, compared with r = 0.23 in the original study. The anterior cingulate association was not consistently recovered. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2024.110532

headline: Nobody passes you the ball. Does your brain register pain?
title: Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion
note: Participants played a virtual ball-toss game. At first they got the ball, then the other players left them out. Researchers compared the two phases to ask whether social distress recruits regions associated with physical pain. A later study of rejection and physical pain found separate multivoxel patterns even in regions activated by both. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms6380

headline: Do traders’ brains sound the alarm before a crash?
title: Irrational exuberance and neural crash warning signals during endogenous experimental market bubbles
note: In an experimental market, volunteers traded an asset whose price they set by buying and selling. The authors compared brain activity with the timing of sales to look for warning signs before the price collapsed.

headline: Can a brain scan predict who will be arrested again?
title: Neuroprediction of future rearrest
note: The authors associated task-related brain activity with future rearrest among released prisoners.

headline: Does the amygdala reveal whether you think society is fair?
title: Amygdala structure and the tendency to regard the social system as legitimate and desirable
note: The study associated amygdala anatomy with system justification.

headline: Can brain anatomy tell you how many Facebook friends you have?
title: Online social network size is reflected in human brain structure
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors associated online social network size with gray matter density.

headline: Can brain activity reveal who chooses to cheat?
title: Patterns of neural activity associated with honest and dishonest moral decisions
note: The study used a task with an opportunity to cheat and measured neural signals.

headline: Is loneliness reflected in the size of a region involved in reading eye gaze?
title: Brain structure links loneliness to social perception
note: The authors related loneliness scores to gray matter volume in the posterior superior temporal sulcus and gaze perception performance.

headline: Does your brain enjoy seeing an unfair player suffer?
title: Empathic neural responses are modulated by the perceived fairness of others
note: Participants observed previously fair or unfair players receiving painful stimulation; the authors related neural responses to perceived fairness and desire for revenge.

headline: Can a teenager's brain predict the next hit song?
title: A neural predictor of cultural popularity
note: Brain responses to songs from a small group of adolescents were correlated with the songs' sales during the following three years.

headline: Do Democrats and Republicans use different brain regions to buy milk and eggs?
title: Differential brain activations between Democrats and Republicans when considering food purchases
note: Reported different brain activations despite no significant difference in food choices.

headline: Are there chocolate buy buttons in the brain?
title: Multiple “buy buttons” in the brain: Forecasting chocolate sales at point-of-sale based on functional brain activation using fMRI
note: The study related fMRI activity to sales of chocolate.

headline: Can scanning 50 smokers predict the performance of 400,000 campaign emails?
title: Functional brain imaging predicts public health campaign success
note: The study linked aggregated fMRI responses to click-through outcomes of an antismoking email campaign.

headline: Can electrical brain stimulation make people more politically conservative?
title: Alteration of Political Belief by Non-invasive Brain Stimulation
note: The authors reported a shift in political belief scores toward conservatism after random-noise stimulation of the prefrontal cortex during exposure to campaign material.

headline: Can a brain scan predict whether your relationship will survive another 40 months?
title: Regional brain activity during early-stage intense romantic love predicted relationship outcomes after 40 months: an fMRI assessment
note: The follow-up compared initial brain scans of six participants still together and six who had separated.

headline: Is a brick wall a message from the universe? Ask an MRI scanner.
title: Is it just a brick wall or a sign from the universe? An fMRI study of supernatural believers and skeptics
note: Compared brain responses of supernatural believers and skeptics viewing pictures that could be interpreted as signs about imagined life events.

headline: Can the location of a brain injury tell how much you care about politics?
title: Effects of focal brain damage on political behaviour across different political ideologies
note: Decades after penetrating head injuries, 124 veterans reported current political interest, news habits, and discussion frequency and recalled their pre-injury behavior. The authors combined lesion locations with a reference connectome to infer a circuit linked to the change in this score. Associations with party affiliation and ideological direction fell short of statistical significance.

headline: Do people at opposite political extremes have more synchronized brains?
title: Politically Extreme Individuals Exhibit Similar Neural Processing Despite Ideological Differences
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers scored extremity from self-reported ideology and compared fMRI time courses during political footage. They reported greater synchrony in posterior superior temporal regions for people with more extreme scores, including pairs from opposite sides. The comparison linked a rating-scale distance to a measure of response similarity during the selected clips.

headline: Can your brainwaves predict how you will vote in an election?
title: Early EEG responses to pre-electoral survey items reflect political attitudes and predict voting behavior
note: The authors recorded EEG as participants read policy statements before the Italian general election and asked them afterward how they voted. A model combining survey answers and an N400 measure fit reported voting behavior better than a survey-only model in the small study sample.

headline: Can a brain scan tell which beliefs you would refuse to sell?
title: The price of your soul: neural evidence for the non-utilitarian representation of sacred values
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: Participants saw value statements in a scanner and later bid for how much money they would accept to sign a statement contradicting a chosen belief. The authors used auction opt-outs to classify values as sacred and linked earlier fMRI differences to rule-based reasoning.

headline: Do people who hate uncertainty have more synchronized brains during political debates?
title: Intolerance of uncertainty modulates brain-to-brain synchrony during politically polarized perception
note: The study related uncertainty questionnaire scores to similarity in fMRI time series across 44 people. Same-side synchrony was strongest during a provocative debate, and the authors interpreted its relationship with intolerance of uncertainty as a clue to how political polarization forms.

headline: Can a brain scan separate patriotism from nationalism?
title: Distinct psychological and neural constructs of patriotism and nationalism
note: Participants rated statements sorted into patriotic or nationalist emotions and beliefs. The authors used principal components and fMRI contrasts to infer distinct constructs, then used a statistical mediation model to link a frontal response to reported tendencies to help other countries.

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether the same generous act came from empathy or from returning a favor?
title: The brain's functional network architecture reveals human motives
note: The researchers induced empathy and reciprocity in separate experimental conditions and compared fMRI connectivity during altruistic choices. They used connectivity to classify the assigned conditions and framed the result as identifying different hidden motives behind the same act. The motive labels came from the experiment.

headline: Can a macaque's brain distinguish whether someone is grabbing food to eat it or put it away?
title: Parietal lobe: from action organization to intention understanding
note: The authors compared single-neuron firing while macaques grasped objects or watched an experimenter grasp them in different action sequences. Neurons fired differently before the next movement. The authors interpreted this as evidence that observation responses contribute to recognizing the actor's intention.

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether someone thinks a hand is picking up a cup to drink or to clear the table?
title: Grasping the intentions of others with one's own mirror neuron system
note: The study compared fMRI responses to grasping, scenes alone, and grasping embedded in scenes suggesting drinking or cleaning. The authors used differences in inferior frontal activation to infer automatic coding of another person's intention. The intended action was signaled by the video context.

headline: Can a brain scan tell how many layers deep you are guessing what other people will do?
title: Neural correlates of depth of strategic reasoning in medial prefrontal cortex
note: Participants played a number-guessing game against human or computer opponents. The researchers assigned levels of strategic reasoning from the numbers players chose and related these labels to prefrontal activity. The levels describe an inferred reasoning process.

headline: Can a brain scan tell when you are thinking about how your moves change an opponent's strategy?
title: Neural correlates of mentalizing-related computations during strategic interactions in humans
note: The researchers fitted competing models to choices in a repeated inspection game. They compared fMRI signals with quantities from a model in which players estimate how their own actions influence an opponent. The proposed beliefs were generated by the fitted model.

headline: Can a brain scan detect whether a private thought is about yourself and whether it feels positive?
title: Brain decoding of spontaneous thought: Predictive modeling of self-relevance and valence using personal narratives
note: The authors trained models while participants read personal and common stories, then applied them during spontaneous thought sampling. They tested predictions against ratings of self-relevance and emotional valence. The targets were subjective scores on two dimensions.

headline: Can an fMRI model tell whether you chose to lie about a shape you had seen?
title: Detecting spontaneous deception in the brain
note: Researchers compared instructed and freely chosen false answers about visual stimuli and tested how fMRI classification transferred across tasks and people. The study framed the results as deception detection, with ground truth defined by stimulus history and answers.

headline: Can a scan distinguish someone who acted out a mock theft from someone who just learned the details?
title: Memory detection using fMRI - does the encoding context matter?
note: The study compared fMRI responses to details of a mock crime across different ways of learning those details. The authors tested whether patterns could distinguish knowledge of the details from how participants acquired that knowledge.

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether an event in a photo actually came from your own life?
title: Decoding fMRI Signatures of Real-world Autobiographical Memory Retrieval
note: Participants wore cameras and later judged sequences of photos from their own lives or from other people's cameras. The strongest classifier result contrasted correctly recognized personal events with correctly rejected novel events, two categories that differ in both prior exposure and subjective recognition.

headline: Can fMRI reveal the personality traits you inferred about someone and predict how you will split money with them?
title: Neural representations of others' traits predict social decisions
note: The study compared similarities in brain responses with warmth and competence ratings of social groups. It linked the orbitofrontal pattern to later money-allocation choices. The proposed personal traits were inferred from group labels and ratings.

headline: Can a scanner infer what someone saw in a dream as they fell asleep?
title: Neural decoding of visual imagery during sleep
note: The researchers woke participants repeatedly around sleep onset and extracted object categories from their verbal reports. Models trained on waking visual responses predicted some of those categories from pre-awakening fMRI. The target was the category label derived from the report.

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether you remember a face or actually saw it before?
title: Detecting individual memories through the neural decoding of memory states and past experience
note: Participants judged whether faces were familiar. The fMRI classifier distinguished subjective recognition states more readily than actual prior exposure when prior exposure and recognition judgments came apart. The study illustrates a difference between decoding a memory judgment and verifying an event.

headline: Can individual neurons reveal what a participant thinks a story character believes?
title: Single-neuronal predictions of others’ beliefs in humans
note: The researchers recorded single neurons while participants answered questions about short narratives, such as where a character would expect to find a moved jar. They used differences in firing across story conditions to infer how neurons represent a character's belief and whether it is true or false. See the recording-location correction. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06263-6

headline: Can a person's representation in the brain be rebuilt by adding up mental states?
title: The brain represents people as the mental states they habitually experience
note: The researchers combined fMRI patterns for individual mental states using ratings of how often a target person would experience each state. They compared the resulting weighted sums with fMRI patterns for thinking about that person.

headline: Can the brain's representations of other minds be reduced to three dimensions?
title: Neural evidence that three dimensions organize mental state representation: Rationality, social impact, and valence
note: The authors proposed dimensions from ratings of mental states and compared the geometry of those ratings with similarities among fMRI patterns during a mental-state task. Three dimensions accounted for part of the similarity structure.

headline: Can a brain scan tell how much you blame someone for an accident?
title: Decoding moral judgments from neural representations of intentions
note: Participants read stories about deliberate or accidental harm. The authors related how distinctly right temporoparietal fMRI patterns separated the story categories to how much participants relied on intention in their moral judgments.

headline: Does a macaque's gaze reveal what it thinks another individual falsely believes?
title: Macaques Exhibit Implicit Gaze Bias Anticipating Others' False-Belief-Driven Actions via Medial Prefrontal Cortex
note: Japanese macaques watched a false-belief scenario, and the researchers measured where they looked in anticipation of another individual's action. They related changes in that gaze bias after a medial prefrontal intervention to implicit belief attribution.

headline: Can a monkey's neurons predict whether its partner will cooperate?
title: Neuronal prediction of opponent's behavior during cooperative social interchange in primates
note: Macaques played a repeated cooperation game while researchers recorded dorsal anterior cingulate neurons. Activity before the partner's move contained information about whether that partner would cooperate or defect, the two choices available in the game.

headline: Can your brain explain why you believe good news about your side of Brexit?
title: Trust in information, political identity and the brain: an interdisciplinary fMRI study
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: Remain supporters rated Brexit messages that varied in whether they favored their side and came from trusted sources. The authors used fMRI contrasts during the task to support an account of misinformation endorsement based on motivated cognition.

headline: Does a powerful political speech make its listeners' brains run in sync?
title: Engaged listeners: shared neural processing of powerful political speeches
note: Listeners heard recordings of speeches by German politicians that had been rated as rhetorically strong or weak. The authors compared correlations across listeners' BOLD time series and interpreted greater synchrony during powerful speeches as evidence of shared engagement.

headline: Can magnetic brain stimulation change how you rate an immigrant who criticizes your country?
title: Neuromodulation of group prejudice and religious belief
note: After a reminder of death, participants rated pro-US and anti-US essays attributed to immigrants and answered religious-belief questions. The study reported a change in ratings of the critical author after stimulation and used these scores to infer a mechanism for defending group beliefs. A preregistered follow-up recovered the positive religious-belief result in the death-reminder comparison. https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsaa153

headline: Can brain lesions be mapped to a circuit for religious fundamentalism?
title: A neural network for religious fundamentalism derived from patients with brain lesions
note: Researchers related fundamentalism questionnaire scores in 190 people with brain lesions to estimated lesion connectivity from a reference connectome. The resulting map was interpreted as a neural network underlying religious fundamentalism.

headline: Can long-running conflict change how the brain responds to someone else's pain?
title: Adolescents growing up amidst intractable conflict attenuate brain response to pain of outgroup
note: Jewish-Israeli and Arab-Palestinian adolescents viewed pain stimuli while MEG responses were recorded. The study reported early somatosensory alpha suppression for both groups of targets and a later rebound only for same-group targets. The authors interpreted the later difference as regulation of empathy during conflict.

headline: Can a dialogue program change teenagers' brainwaves and predict their peacemaking as adults?
title: Dialogue intervention for youth amidst intractable conflict attenuates neural prejudice response and promotes adults’ peacemaking
note: The trial measured changes in occipital alpha activity after a youth dialogue program. The authors interpreted the signal as implicit prejudice and related adolescent data to self-reported peacebuilding engagement in a follow-up seven years later.

headline: Can paradoxical messages make people's brains process a political conflict more alike?
title: The paradoxical brain: paradoxes impact conflict perspectives through increased neural alignment
note: The authors compared MEG alignment before and after a messaging intervention on the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Alignment increased within the intervention group for political narratives on both sides. They fitted separate canonical correlation models by group and based the neural finding on within-group comparisons.

headline: Does a racial stereotype make the brain represent a tool more like a gun?
title: Racial stereotypes bias the neural representation of objects towards perceived weapons
note: After viewing face primes, the imaging analysis compared the response pattern for tools with a response pattern for guns. The authors treated greater similarity after Black face primes as evidence of a perceptual shift and related it to response-time differences in a weapon-identification task.

headline: Can an MRI photo task explain why an interracial conversation affects attention?
title: An fMRI investigation of the impact of interracial contact on executive function
note: The authors related an implicit race-bias measure and Stroop performance after an interracial interaction to prefrontal responses recorded while viewing unfamiliar faces in a separate session. They interpreted these associations as evidence that some interracial interactions draw down executive resources.

headline: Does the amygdala react differently when a face appears for just 30 milliseconds?
title: Separable neural components in the processing of black and white faces
note: The study compared responses to Black and White faces at two exposure durations. A short-exposure amygdala contrast and results from an implicit association task were used to infer automatic evaluations and their regulation at longer exposures.

headline: Can assigning someone to a team change how their amygdala responds to strangers?
title: The neural substrates of in-group bias: a functional magnetic resonance imaging investigation
note: Participants were randomly assigned to mixed-race teams and shown unfamiliar teammate and rival faces. The authors linked greater activation for teammates to automatic group evaluation and treated an orbitofrontal response as a statistical mediator of face-liking ratings.

headline: Does watching a needle prick register differently depending on the race of the person in the video?
title: Racial bias reduces empathic sensorimotor resonance with other-race pain
note: Participants watched videos of a needle entering hands of different skin colors. The authors used TMS-evoked muscle responses as a measure of sensorimotor resonance and related the response difference to implicit racial-bias scores, interpreting it as reduced empathy.

headline: Can a hormone measurement and a brain scan explain retaliation against someone uninvolved?
title: A neurobiological association of revenge propensity during intergroup conflict
note: In a laboratory group-conflict task, the authors related salivary oxytocin, medial prefrontal responses while viewing pain, and decisions to assign painful stimulation to members of another group. They proposed that the statistical mediation links the laboratory pattern to the spread of retaliation.

headline: Do individualism, conservatism, and radicalism show up in different parts of the brain?
title: Individualism, conservatism, and radicalism as criteria for processing political beliefs: a parametric fMRI study
note: The authors applied multidimensional scaling to political statements, labeled three dimensions, and estimated how each dimension covaried with brain activity during statement judgments. The proposed neural distinctions depend on the coordinates derived for that particular set of statements.

headline: Do dads with smaller testicles do more childcare?
title: Testicular volume is inversely correlated with nurturing-related brain activity in human fathers
note: The authors linked testicular volume to reported childcare and to a father's ventral tegmental response to photos of his own child. They interpreted the correlations as evidence of a trade-off between mating and parenting. The analysis compared differences across fathers at a single period in their lives.

headline: Can the size of your amygdala give away the size of your social circle?
title: Amygdala volume and social network size in humans
note: The authors correlated amygdala volume with questionnaire-based counts of social contacts and groups. A follow-up using 7-tesla MRI in 128 adults found small estimates and inconclusive support for the offline-network relationship. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13415-024-01185-w

headline: Can a robot make you feel that an invisible person is standing behind you?
title: Neurological and robot-controlled induction of an apparition
note: The authors combined lesion observations with a robotic task that altered the timing of touch relative to participants' movements. Some participants reported a presence nearby. The authors interpreted the experience as a misattribution of signals generated by one's own body.

headline: Can a weak magnetic field make someone sense an unseen presence?
title: Experimental facilitation of the sensed presence: possible intercalation between the hemispheres induced by complex magnetic fields
venue: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
note: The authors compared reports of a presence during different weak magnetic field conditions and proposed a mechanism involving the two hemispheres. A double-blind sham-controlled study with 89 people did not reproduce the field effect and found that suggestibility predicted reported experiences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neulet.2004.10.057

headline: Do people who hear voices also hear a tone the lab never played?
title: Pavlovian Conditioning-Induced Hallucinations Result from Overweighting of Perceptual Priors
note: Participants learned an association between a visual cue and a tone. The voice-hearing groups, which included self-described clairaudient psychics, more often reported a tone on trials without one. The authors used fMRI and a computational model to link those reports to the weighting of expectations.

headline: Could a robot-induced sense of someone nearby reveal who is prone to presence hallucinations in Parkinson's disease?
title: Robot-induced hallucinations in Parkinson's disease depend on altered sensorimotor processing in fronto-temporal network
note: The study compared reports triggered by delayed tactile feedback and mapped associated brain connectivity. It used the laboratory sensation of someone nearby as a probe of spontaneous presence hallucinations in Parkinson's disease.

headline: Can a camera and a touch make you feel as if you are sitting outside your body?
title: The experimental induction of out-of-body experiences
note: Participants viewed their bodies from a displaced camera perspective while receiving synchronized or unsynchronized touch. Reports and skin-conductance responses to a threat near the camera were used to infer where participants felt located.

headline: Can watching a video of your body shift where you think you are standing?
title: Video ergo sum: manipulating bodily self-consciousness
note: Participants viewed a virtual body during synchronous or asynchronous stroking and then indicated where they had been standing. The authors interpreted a shift toward the seen body as a change in the perceived location of the self.

headline: Do you remember an encounter less clearly if you experienced it from outside your body?
title: Out-of-body-induced hippocampal amnesia
note: Participants experienced staged social encounters from different camera perspectives. The authors compared later recall and hippocampal fMRI responses and interpreted the difference as evidence that perceived bodily location changes how episodic memories form.

headline: Can brain damage map spirituality onto a circuit centered in the midbrain?
title: A Neural Circuit for Spirituality and Religiosity Derived From Patients With Brain Lesions
note: The authors linked spirituality and religiosity measures in two lesion cohorts to connectivity estimated from a reference connectome. Their maps converged near the periaqueductal gray, which they interpreted as the center of a shared circuit.

headline: Is religious or spiritual importance reflected in the thickness of the cortex?
title: Neuroanatomical Correlates of Religiosity and Spirituality: A Study in Adults at High and Low Familial Risk for Depression
note: The study linked personal ratings of the importance of religion or spirituality to MRI estimates of cortical thickness in 103 adults. The authors proposed a relationship to resilience against depression, drawing on a comparison by familial risk.

headline: Can looking at the Virgin Mary change how painful an electric shock feels?
title: An fMRI study measuring analgesia enhanced by religion as a belief system
note: Practicing Catholics and nonreligious participants viewed religious or secular images during painful stimulation. Group differences in pain ratings and fMRI contrasts were used to infer that religious belief can change pain through reinterpretation.

headline: Do stronger religious convictions change the EEG response to an error?
title: Neural markers of religious conviction
note: The authors related religiosity measures to error-related electrical activity and performance during a Stroop task. They used a smaller error-related signal to support an account of religious conviction as a buffer against anxiety.

headline: Can long-term Buddhist meditators generate unusually synchronized gamma waves?
title: Long-term meditators self-induce high-amplitude gamma synchrony during mental practice
note: The researchers compared scalp EEG from experienced Buddhist practitioners and controls during meditation. They interpreted gamma power and phase-synchrony differences as possible effects of mental training, using a comparison between groups with different training histories.

headline: Why did the most experienced meditators show less activation in an attention network than other experts?
title: Neural correlates of attentional expertise in long-term meditation practitioners
note: During concentration meditation, fMRI activation in attention-related regions showed an inverted-U pattern across levels of experience. The authors used the group differences to propose that more extensive practice changes how attentional resources are recruited.

headline: Does a burst of gamma activity suggest consciousness as the human brain is dying?
title: Surge of neurophysiological coupling and connectivity of gamma oscillations in the dying human brain
note: Two of four comatose patients showed a surge in gamma activity and connectivity after withdrawal of ventilatory support. The authors considered a possible link with conscious processing. The records contained EEG measurements from the patients’ final moments and no firsthand reports of what they experienced.

headline: Can a rat's brain waves after cardiac arrest explain vivid near-death experiences?
title: Surge of neurophysiological coherence and connectivity in the dying brain
note: EEG in rats showed a brief increase in gamma synchrony after induced cardiac arrest. The authors proposed that organized activity after arrest could provide a framework for studying unusually vivid experiences reported by human survivors.

headline: Can brain-network changes track the reported intensity of an experience under psilocybin?
title: Psilocybin desynchronizes the human brain
note: Repeated fMRI scans in a small group of adults showed broad changes in functional connectivity, including in the default mode network. The authors related the size of those changes to questionnaire ratings of the subjective experience.

headline: Does the brain align more with a movie or music during a psychedelic experience?
title: Psychedelics align brain activity with context
note: The authors recorded fMRI and EEG in 62 adults during rest and during meditation, music, and film conditions before and during a psilocybin session. They reported context-dependent alignment of brain activity and interpreted it in relation to experiences of a less distinct boundary between self and surroundings.

headline: Can changes in brain connectivity explain a feeling of losing your sense of self?
title: Neural correlates of the LSD experience revealed by multimodal neuroimaging
note: The authors measured imaging differences between LSD and placebo sessions. A change in connectivity between parahippocampal and retrosplenial regions correlated with self-reported ego dissolution. The study used that correlation to identify a candidate neural correlate of the experience.

headline: Does seeing a picture of your ex engage the same brain regions as a hot probe?
title: Social rejection shares somatosensory representations with physical pain
note: Participants recalled an unwanted breakup while viewing a photo of their ex and separately received painful heat. The authors used overlap in fMRI activation to argue for shared somatosensory representations. A subsequent study using the same tasks found distinct multivoxel patterns even in regions activated by both. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms6380

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether someone is being seen as less than human?
title: Dehumanizing the Lowest of the Low: Neuroimaging Responses to Extreme Out-Groups
note: Ten participants viewed photos assigned to stereotype categories, including photos of people experiencing homelessness or addiction. The authors treated lack of medial prefrontal activation in that condition, alongside greater activation in the insula and amygdala, as evidence of dehumanization. The conclusion about dehumanization came from the imaging contrast.

headline: Can brain scans tell whether you give to charity out of pure altruism?
title: Neural responses to taxation and voluntary giving reveal motives for charitable donations
note: In a task with real transfers to a food bank, reward-related regions responded to mandatory transfers and responded more to voluntary giving. The authors used those contrasts to infer pure altruism and warm glow as motives. The transfers were observed in dollars, while the distinction between motives rested on the interpretation of the imaging contrasts.

headline: Does your brain automatically decide whom to trust from a photo?
title: Automatic and intentional brain responses during evaluation of trustworthiness of faces
note: Amygdala and insula responses were correlated with rated untrustworthiness even during a different face-judgment task. The authors interpreted this as automatic social evaluation. Trustworthiness here was an impression from a photograph, based on participants' ratings.

headline: Do lonely people see the world differently, according to their brain scans?
title: Lonely Individuals Process the World in Idiosyncratic Ways
note: The authors correlated loneliness questionnaire scores with how dissimilar 66 students' fMRI time series were while they watched the same videos. The headline claim about experiencing the world differently was based on similarity between response time series.

headline: Does the amygdala get used to lying before your lies get bigger?
title: The brain adapts to dishonesty
note: In an estimation task with incentives to mislead a partner, smaller amygdala responses from one trial to the next predicted larger subsequent increases in self-serving misreporting. The authors interpreted the signal change as an adaptation mechanism supporting escalation.

headline: Can a brain scan predict whether a soccer fan would take an electric shock for a rival fan?
title: Neural responses to ingroup and outgroup members' suffering predict individual differences in costly helping
note: Soccer fans watched supporters of their own or a rival club receive painful stimulation and could volunteer to take pain in their place. The authors linked different fMRI responses to willingness to help the two groups and interpreted them as neural predictors of group-dependent helping.

headline: Can your brain signal when you are about to cave to the crowd?
title: Reinforcement learning signal predicts social conformity
note: Participants rated faces, saw purported group ratings and then rated the faces again. Brain responses to disagreement predicted shifts toward the group rating. The authors interpreted the response as a reinforcement-learning error signal for conformity.

headline: Does your brain group your friends and acquaintances apart from celebrities?
title: Self-Other Representation in the Social Brain Reflects Social Connection
note: Participants judged traits for themselves, acquaintances, close contacts and celebrities. The authors clustered fMRI patterns from those judgments and interpreted the clusters and their relationship to loneliness as a neural organization of social connection.

headline: Does it feel better to watch someone else get paid when you started out richer?
title: Neural evidence for inequality-averse social preferences
note: The study gave one member of each pair a larger initial payment, then recorded fMRI responses to transfers benefiting either person. The authors interpreted differences in responses to the transfers as evidence of a preference for reducing inequality.

headline: Does the same payout register differently in your brain when someone else gets more?
title: Social comparison affects reward-related brain activity in the human ventral striatum
note: Pairs completed an estimation task in adjacent scanners. The other player's payout changed the ventral striatal response to payment feedback. The analysis treated that signal as reward processing, while the outcome measured in the scanner was a BOLD response to the feedback.

headline: Can a brain scan tell how harshly you would punish a crime?
title: The neural correlates of third-party punishment
note: Participants assigned punishments to written scenarios that varied in severity and the offender's responsibility. The authors related punishment scores and scenario types to different BOLD responses and proposed a common mechanism linking criminal judgments to economic norm enforcement.

headline: Can brain scans tell who follows the rules only when there is a penalty?
title: The neural signature of social norm compliance
note: The experiment compared monetary allocations with and without possible punishment. Changes in allocations were correlated with activity in lateral prefrontal areas, and orbitofrontal activity was also correlated with Machiavellianism scores. The authors framed the contrasts as a neural signature of norm compliance.

headline: Does your brain start anticipating trust 14 seconds earlier once it knows your partner?
title: Getting to know you: reputation and trust in a two-person economic exchange
note: In a multiround exchange game, dorsal striatal response magnitude tracked a player's next decision to trust, and the timing of a response peak shifted by 14 seconds across rounds. The authors interpreted these measurements as signals of the intention to trust and the development of reputations.

headline: Can a good reputation make your brain tune out a bad deal?
title: Perceptions of moral character modulate the neural systems of reward during the trust game
note: Participants read character descriptions and then played a trust game. The caudate response distinguished favorable from unfavorable feedback most clearly for the neutral partner. The authors interpreted the contrast as evidence that moral impressions reduce reliance on feedback during learning.

headline: Can a nasal spray keep you trusting someone who already let you down?
title: Oxytocin Shapes the Neural Circuitry of Trust and Trust Adaptation in Humans
note: In a placebo-controlled trust game, the groups differed in investment adjustments after feedback about breaches of trust. The authors related that difference to BOLD contrasts in the amygdala, midbrain and dorsal striatum and proposed fear and feedback learning as explanations.

headline: Can a brain scan tell whether you kept your word to avoid feeling guilty?
title: Triangulating the neural, psychological, and economic bases of guilt aversion
note: A trust-game model defined guilt in terms of falling short of a partner's expected return. The authors linked behavior consistent with that fitted model to brain activation and interpreted it as evidence about the neural machinery through which guilt sustains cooperation.

headline: Does money look less rewarding to your brain if someone else gets shocked?
title: Moral transgressions corrupt neural representations of value
note: Participants weighed money against shocks delivered to themselves or another person. The analysis related imaging signals to modeled profit and pain values and interpreted condition differences as a change in how the brain represents the value of ill-gotten gains.

headline: When you turn down an unfair offer, can a brain scan tell whether emotion won?
title: The neural basis of economic decision-making in the Ultimatum Game
note: Participants accepted or rejected proposed splits of money. Larger anterior insula responses accompanied rejected unfair offers, which the authors took as evidence of emotional involvement in bargaining. Rejection was observed directly, while the emotional explanation came from the mapping of activity to a psychological process.

headline: Can a brainwave detect when a politician says something out of character?
title: The neural dynamics of political socio-pragmatic violations: an ERP study
note: The study measured time-locked EEG responses when political utterances did or did not fit expectations about the speaker or context.

headline: Do supporters’ brainwaves react differently to emotional faces from their own party?
title: Neural responses to emotional displays by politicians: differential mu and alpha suppression patterns in response to in-party and out-party leaders
note: The researchers compared EEG mu and alpha suppression while participants saw politicians’ emotional displays. The proposed interpretation concerns resonance with political leaders.

headline: Can the brainwaves of voters reveal how they will vote?
title: Neurodynamics of an election
note: The study measured EEG in 32 Brazilian voters in the five days before an election and compared neural responses to candidates with voting preferences.

headline: Does frontal EEG activity separate people on opposite sides of a vaccine mandate?
title: Cognitive–Affective Dynamics of Political Attitude Polarization: EEG-Based Behavioral Evidence from a COVID-19 Vaccine Mandate Task
note: The authors used a vaccine-mandate task and EEG to compare responses across attitudes. This measures task responses in the study sample.

headline: Can EEG track how political values change the way you hear a sentence?
title: Individual Differences in Political Ideology and Disgust Sensitivity Affect Real-Time Spoken Language Comprehension
note: The study related ideology and disgust-sensitivity scores to event-related potentials during spoken language comprehension.

headline: Do the brain's moral foundations light up differently for liberals and conservatives?
title: Moral foundations elicit shared and dissociable cortical activation modulated by political ideology
note: The researchers compared fMRI activity across moral-vignette categories and related activation patterns to ideology.

headline: Can one brain network tell when a voter is reasoning in favor of their side?
title: Tracking politically motivated reasoning in the brain: the role of mentalizing, value-encoding, and error detection networks
note: The authors related neural responses during political evaluations to behavioral measures of politically motivated reasoning.

headline: Do brains synchronize when a discussion makes political opinions less extreme?
title: Interbrain Synchrony Mitigates Extremism Within Echo Chambers
venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
note: The study relates interpersonal neural synchrony in a group discussion to shifts in measured political extremity.

headline: Can an acquired political identity change neural responses in a trust game?
title: How Do Acquired Political Identities Influence Our Neural Processing toward Others within the Context of a Trust Game?
note: The authors measured neural responses while participants made trust decisions involving people with different political identities.

headline: Can a brain response to someone else’s suffering be linked to ideological values?
title: Ideological values are parametrically associated with empathy neural response to vicarious suffering
note: The analysis related questionnaire measures of ideological values to neural responses to scenes of others suffering.

headline: Can a face-processing brain area distinguish people with high and low xenophobia scores?
title: Fusiform Activity Distinguishes Between Subjects With Low and High Xenophobic Attitudes Toward Refugees
note: The study compared fMRI response patterns between groups defined by attitudes toward refugees.

headline: Do brain responses to someone in pain vary with respondents’ attitudes toward refugees?
title: Refugees welcome? Empathy attenuates effects of xenophobia on neuronal responses to in-group and out-group suffering
note: The researchers modeled neural responses using in-group and out-group labels, xenophobia scores, and measures of empathy.

headline: Can a neural response pick up small reservations about immigration among people who support it?
title: Supportive but biased: Perceptual neural intergroup bias is sensitive to minor reservations about supporting outgroup immigration
note: The authors related a neural contrast between groups to variation in reported support for immigration.

headline: Can activity in the precuneus predict attitudes across the Israeli–Arab divide?
title: Attitudes towards the outgroup are predicted by activity in the precuneus in Arabs and Israelis
note: The authors related fMRI contrasts during a social judgment task to questionnaire attitudes about the outgroup.

headline: Does a brain scan show different reactions to misfortune on opposite sides of a conflict?
title: Social cognition in members of conflict groups: behavioural and neural responses in Arabs, Israelis and South Americans to each other's misfortunes
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: Participants read scenarios about misfortunes affecting different groups. The authors compared behavioral ratings and fMRI responses.

headline: Can brain rhythms while watching others in pain indicate support for peacebuilding?
title: Neural rhythmic underpinnings of intergroup bias: implications for peace-building attitudes and dialogue
note: The paper links neural oscillatory responses to in-group and out-group pain with reported peacebuilding attitudes.

headline: Can scalp EEG pick up conflict when someone reads misleading vaccine claims?
title: Neural mechanisms of cognitive conflict: processing COVID-19 vaccine misinformation
note: The researchers measured event-related EEG responses to vaccine claims and interpreted selected contrasts as cognitive conflict.

headline: Do some brain lesions shift where people place themselves on a political scale?
title: Toward a neuropsychology of political orientation: exploring ideology in patients with frontal and midbrain lesions
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The study compared political orientation measures across focal brain lesion locations and comparison participants, reporting an association with dorsolateral prefrontal damage.

headline: Can children's brainwaves on a conflict task reveal their parents’ political ideology?
title: Associations between parental ideology and neural sensitivity to cognitive conflict in children
note: The authors linked children's event-related EEG measures in a cognitive-control task to political ideology reported by their parents.

headline: Does the brain show signs of confirmation bias while watching videos about Korean politics?
title: People see what they want to see: an EEG study
note: Participants watched videos about North Korea policy and social welfare. The authors related EEG and self-report responses to agreement with the videos.

headline: Does the brain flag a statement that goes against your political or moral values before you finish hearing it?
title: Right or wrong? The brain's fast response to morally objectionable statements
note: The study compared EEG responses to spoken statements, including disputed social issues, between respondents with different value commitments.

headline: Would a scan show why people stay with a political belief even after hearing a counterargument?
title: Neural correlates of belief change in political and non-political domains among left-wing individuals confronted with counterarguments
note: Participants recruited for their left-wing views heard counterarguments while undergoing fMRI. The study compared political and nonpolitical beliefs and associated brain responses.

headline: Can a scan separate voting because your vote might count from voting for its own sake?
title: The Neuroeconomics of Voting: Neural Evidence of Different Sources of Utility in Voting
venue: Journal of Neuroscience, Psychology, and Economics
note: Participants voted on a monetary transfer to charity in the laboratory. The authors compared neural responses across conditions designed to distinguish instrumental and expressive motives.

headline: Can a brain scan distinguish moral conviction from support for political violence?
title: The Dark Side of Morality – Neural Mechanisms Underpinning Moral Convictions and Support for Violence
note: The authors used neural responses and ratings from a task involving sociopolitical scenarios to examine the relationship between moral conviction and endorsement of violence.

headline: Do liberal and conservative participants process racially ambiguous faces differently in a scanner?
title: The neural basis of ideological differences in race categorization
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The study examined neural responses while participants categorized faces and linked them to political ideology scores.

headline: Can an fMRI contrast explain how subtle racial cues affect judgments about welfare applicants?
title: The neural mechanisms of race priming in American politics
note: Twenty-five participants rated government-aid applicants following explicit or masked face cues. The paper models contrasts between conditions as evidence about the processing of racial cues.

headline: Can the brain tell when AI-generated campaign images have been labeled as true or false?
title: Do truthfulness notifications influence perceptions of AI-generated political images? A cognitive investigation with EEG
venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
note: The authors compared EEG and judgments across truthfulness labels on AI-generated images with political content.

headline: Does climate anxiety have its own pattern in the brain?
title: Climate change on the brain: Neural correlates of climate anxiety
note: The study analyzed whether responses to climate imagery varied with scores on a climate-anxiety questionnaire.

headline: Can environmentalism be inferred from resting brain connections?
title: Intrinsic functional connectivity correlates of pro-environmentalism
note: The study related resting-state connectivity to measures of environmental attitudes and behavior.

headline: Can gray-matter differences explain why some people behave more sustainably?
title: Individual differences in structural neuroanatomy related to pro-environmental behavior
note: The authors used structural brain data to model individual differences in measures of environmentally protective behavior.

headline: Do persuasive climate messages sound different to the brain when they appeal to duty or personal gain?
title: Neural bases of goal-frame theory: Assessing the nature and persuasion of normative, hedonic, and gain environmental messages
note: The authors compared brain responses to environmental messages framed around norms, pleasure or gain and related neural measures to persuasion.

headline: Can activity in lateral prefrontal cortex explain how often people say they act sustainably?
title: Frequency of everyday pro-environmental behaviour is explained by baseline activation in lateral prefrontal cortex
note: The researchers related baseline prefrontal activity to self-reported everyday environmental behavior.

headline: Can an EEG response tell when a person thinks a tax authority is legitimate?
title: Coercive and legitimate authority impact tax honesty: evidence from behavioral and ERP experiments
note: Participants made tax-related decisions in an experiment. The authors compared event-related potentials across authority conditions and related them to reported income.

headline: Do tax decisions evoke different brainwaves depending on how the tax is framed?
title: Social frame and tax compliance modulate electrophysiological and autonomic responses following tax-related decisions
note: Thirty self-employed participants completed a public-goods game. The researchers related EEG and autonomic responses to the social framing and measures of tax compliance.

headline: Does preferring a more equal society depend on imagining yourself in someone else’s position?
title: Human pursuance of equality hinges on mental processes of projecting oneself into the perspectives of others and into future situations
note: Participants chose income-redistribution rules with or without knowledge of their own income class. The authors interpreted activation differences as evidence about perspective taking and thinking about future situations.

headline: Can insula activity tell who will redistribute more in an economic game?
title: Neural basis of egalitarian behavior
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers linked fMRI responses to pictures of people in need to choices in a redistribution task and interpreted activity in the insula in terms of egalitarian behavior.

headline: Does the brain put the trade-off between equality and efficiency in different places?
title: The right and the good: distributive justice and neural encoding of equity and efficiency
note: The authors estimated fMRI responses during decisions about allocating food to children and used a fitted model to assess equity and efficiency.

headline: Can brain scans explain how people respond to testimony about apartheid?
title: Empathy and moral emotions in post-apartheid South Africa: an fMRI investigation
note: The paper compares fMRI and emotional ratings while South African participants view testimony about apartheid-era experiences.

headline: Can brainwaves during emotional videos reveal how empathy varies with racial prejudice?
title: Intergroup differences in the sharing of emotive states: neural evidence of an empathy gap
note: The authors compared EEG responses to emotional displays by members of racial in-groups and out-groups and related them to measures of prejudice.

headline: Can an fMRI scan show how voters guess what their candidate believes as election day approaches?
title: Ascribing beliefs to ingroup and outgroup political candidates: neural correlates of perspective-taking, issue importance and days until the election
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The authors analyzed fMRI responses while Obama and McCain supporters inferred candidate positions, using issue salience and time until the election as predictors.

headline: Can a scan show how political uncertainty changes reactions to politicians who break with their party?
title: Political uncertainty moderates neural evaluation of incongruent policy positions
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers compared neural responses during evaluations of policy positions that did or did not fit a candidate’s party and examined political uncertainty as a moderator.

headline: Can a brain scan predict how much a corruption story will distance you from your party?
title: Neural Predictors of Changes in Party Closeness after Exposure to Corruption Messages: An fMRI Study
note: The authors related fMRI responses to corruption messages to changes in reported party closeness.

headline: Do beliefs about the economy change how brains process messages about political corruption?
title: Modulating the Neural Bases of Political Communications: Political Involvement and Perception of the Economic Situation
note: The authors used fMRI during political messages and tested whether self-reported political involvement and perception of the economy moderated contrasts.

headline: Can mindfulness change the brain’s response to polarizing political videos?
title: Examining emotion reactivity to politically polarizing media in a randomized controlled trial of mindfulness training versus active coping training
note: The study compared fNIRS responses to polarizing clips across mindfulness and active-coping training and related them to emotional ratings.

headline: Can EEG suggest voters remember political events that never happened?
title: Event-related potential evidence suggesting voters remember political events that never happened
note: Researchers compared EEG responses to accurately remembered candidate positions and positions participants misattributed to candidates. They interpreted similar memory-related signals as evidence consistent with false memories.

headline: Can a focus group’s brainwaves forecast which startup pitch raises money?
title: Predicting entrepreneur fundraising success from focus group EEG data
note: Twenty-eight volunteers watched investor pitches. The authors related frontal EEG asymmetry in the first ten seconds and similarity between viewers’ signals to investment interest, deal outcomes and deal sizes.

headline: Can watching marriage scenes in a scanner tell how happy a couple is?
title: Neural synchronization predicts marital satisfaction
note: The authors compared fMRI response similarity in spouses and randomly paired people watching videos about married life. They then used synchrony measures to predict questionnaire scores for marital satisfaction.

headline: Can the resting brain connections of an entire village reveal who is friends with whom?
title: Similarity in functional brain connectivity at rest predicts interpersonal closeness in the social network of an entire village
note: The authors measured friendship by social-network reports in a village. They related people’s distance in that network to the similarity of their resting-state functional connectivity.

headline: Does Euler’s identity share a beauty region with art and music?
title: The experience of mathematical beauty and its neural correlates
note: Fifteen mathematicians rated formulas. The authors found that medial orbitofrontal BOLD activity tracked the individual beauty ratings and compared the region to prior aesthetic results.

headline: Can a scan tell whether you will add or subtract before you report deciding?
title: Predicting free choices for abstract intentions
note: The authors decoded add-versus-subtract choices from prefrontal and parietal fMRI patterns up to four seconds before the reported decision. The timing comparison used participants’ own reports of when they decided.

headline: Can a scan predict which fabric softener you will take home?
title: Latent preference representation in the human brain for scented products: Effects of novelty and familiarity
note: Twenty-five participants smelled three fabric softeners during fMRI before testing them at home. The authors used initial fMRI patterns to decode which product each person later chose.

headline: Can a small group’s brain scans predict demand for appliances carrying an Energy Star label?
title: Neural responses clarify how ecolabels promote sustainable purchases
note: The authors related nucleus accumbens activity during purchasing tasks to individual choices and group-averaged activity to stated choices in a national survey.

headline: Can a trailer-viewing focus group’s EEG predict box-office revenue?
title: Your Brain on the Movies: A Computational Approach for Predicting Box-office Performance from Viewer’s Brain Responses to Movie Trailers
note: The authors related EEG during movie trailers to the films’ actual opening and subsequent box-office performance.

headline: Can a neural network trained on real objects tell which categories you dreamed about?
title: Hierarchical Neural Representation of Dreamed Objects Revealed by Brain Decoding with Deep Neural Network Features
note: The authors used decoders trained on waking fMRI to estimate visual features from sleep fMRI. They scored decoded features against object categories derived from dream reports.

headline: Does a Rembrandt look different to your brain after someone calls it a fake?
title: Human Cortical Activity Evoked by the Assignment of Authenticity when Viewing Works of Art
note: The experiment assigned authenticity labels to portraits and tested whether the designation changed fMRI responses during viewing.

headline: Do meaningful coincidences show up in how the resting brain connects?
title: MRI resting-state signature of the propensity to experience meaningful coincidences: a functional coupling analysis
note: The researchers related a self-reported tendency to experience meaningful coincidences to resting-state fMRI coupling.

headline: Can resting brain activity tell whether you decide to forgive or actually feel forgiveness?
title: Spontaneous brain activity associated with individual differences in decisional and emotional forgiveness.
note: The researchers related spontaneous fMRI activity to separate measures of decisional and emotional forgiveness.

headline: Does prefrontal activity explain how grit turns into better grades?
title: Grit and the brain: spontaneous activity of the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex mediates the relationship between the trait grit and academic performance
note: The authors related resting fMRI activity to grit and academic performance using a mediation model.

headline: From two lucid dreams, can fMRI tell what makes a dreamer self-aware?
title: Neural Correlates of Dream Lucidity Obtained from Contrasting Lucid versus Non-Lucid REM Sleep: A Combined EEG/fMRI Case Study
note: Of four recruited lucid dreamers, one produced two lucid REM episodes suitable for fMRI analysis. The authors interpreted activation differences relative to nonlucid REM as a return of reflective cognition.

headline: Does an asset bubble push traders’ brains into a wishful-thinking mode?
title: Neural basis of economic bubble behavior.
note: Participants traded in a virtual exchange containing a stock with a preset bubble-like price trajectory. The authors interpreted fMRI connectivity during the bubble as a possible contributor to impaired control and wishful thinking.

headline: Can your brain scan predict what a friend wants to buy?
title: Neural Synchrony and Consumer Behavior: Predicting Friends' Behavior in Real-World Social Networks
note: The authors estimated functional connectivity during naturalistic viewing and used it to model friends’ product purchase intentions. The outcome was stated intention.

headline: Does the basal ganglia explain why a beat makes you want to move?
title: The sensation of groove engages motor and reward networks.
note: Listeners rated pleasure and the urge to move while hearing rhythms of different complexity. The authors linked those ratings to fMRI activity in basal ganglia regions.

headline: Can the connections between hearing and reward areas forecast your musical chills?
title: State-dependent connectivity in auditory-reward networks predicts peak pleasure experiences to music
note: The researchers used fMRI connectivity to predict reported chills and measures such as skin conductance within their music-listening sample.

headline: Can a brain scan tell musical wonder from transcendence?
title: Mapping Aesthetic Musical Emotions in the Brain
note: The authors compared fMRI responses across reported aesthetic emotions during music listening and interpreted the patterns in terms of distinct networks, with overlaps for wonder and transcendence.

headline: Do musical goosebumps have their own brainwave pattern?
title: Cortical Patterns of Pleasurable Musical Chills Revealed by High-Density EEG
note: The authors compared dense-array EEG during self-reported chills and other levels of musical pleasure. They interpreted the spectral differences as signatures of musical reward.

headline: Does a favorite song act on the same opioid system as a primary reward?
title: Pleasurable music activates cerebral µ-opioid receptors: a combined PET-fMRI study
venue: European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging
note: The authors used PET and fMRI during pleasurable music listening and interpreted variation in an opioid-receptor measure as evidence that the system also governs aesthetic reward.

headline: Can white-matter wiring tell who gets goosebumps from music?
title: Brain connectivity reflects human aesthetic responses to music
note: Diffusion MRI tract estimates differed between listeners who frequently report musical chills and matched controls. The paper interpreted this as variation in auditory access to reward systems.

headline: Does a suspenseful story light up your brain’s prediction machinery?
title: Reading a Suspenseful Literary Text Activates Brain Areas Related to Social Cognition and Predictive Inference
note: Participants read passages and rated their suspense. The authors used the association between ratings and fMRI activity to infer that suspense depends on social cognition and predictive inference.

headline: Does finding a line poetic recruit a tolerance-for-uncertainty circuit?
title: "Shall I compare thee": The neural basis of literary awareness, and its benefits to cognition.
note: The researchers scanned people reading literary passages and related ratings of poeticness and reappraisal to activity. They interpreted a caudate association in terms of tolerance of uncertainty.

headline: Can an oxygenation signal identify the moment a poem turns beautiful?
title: Neural dynamics of aesthetic appreciation: fNIRS evidence from poetry reading.
note: The authors used fNIRS while participants read poetry and linked a later phase of cortical activity to appreciation ratings and possible memory, imagination and empathy processes.

headline: Can electrical stimulation make a painting look more beautiful?
title: The world can look better: enhancing beauty experience with brain stimulation
note: The experiment compared aesthetic ratings after different stimulation conditions. The authors reported higher ratings for representational images after anodal stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

headline: Can reading an art label switch off part of the work your brain does on a painting?
title: Functional neuroanatomy of the perception of modern art: A DC-EEG study on the influence of stylistic information on aesthetic experience.
note: The researchers supplied stylistic information about modern art and reported weaker left-hemisphere slow cortical potentials, which they interpreted as reduced verbal processing.

headline: Do painters mentally replay their brushstrokes when they see their own work?
title: How artists experience their own art
note: The authors compared responses to artists’ own work and other paintings and interpreted sensorimotor activity as reactivation of the gestures involved in making the art.

headline: Do audiences’ brainwaves line up more when they watch a dance together in person?
title: Delta-band audience brain synchrony tracks engagement with live and recorded dance
note: The authors compared EEG similarities during live or recorded dance with engagement measures and reported the strongest synchrony in the live group setting.

headline: When dancers move in sync, do spectators’ brains follow?
title: Movement synchrony among dance performers predicts brain synchrony among dance spectators
note: The study related the coordination of dancers’ movements to similarities in spectators’ EEG and examined variation with dance expertise and enjoyment.

headline: What happens in your brain when Charlie Chaplin lands a joke?
title: Intracranial study in humans: Neural spectral changes during watching comedy movie of Charlie Chaplin.
note: The study analyzed intracranial EEG during a Chaplin comedy and used frequency-specific activity to infer how humor appreciation is distributed across the brain.

headline: Does a cartoon punchline change regions depending on its kind of logic?
title: Cognitive humor processing: different logical mechanisms in nonverbal cartoons--an fMRI study
note: The researchers compared brain responses to nonverbal cartoons with different kinds of punchline, interpreting the fMRI contrasts as distinct routes to understanding humor.

headline: Does the amygdala send different signals for a funny joke and a creative idea?
title: Amygdala‐frontoparietal effective connectivity in creativity and humor processing
note: The authors fit a model of directed coupling during tasks involving typical and atypical jokes or creative uses and interpreted the estimated connections as distinct appreciation mechanisms.

headline: Can a brain response tell whether you are looking at Dalí or Picasso?
title: Neural art appraisal of painter: Dali or Picasso?
note: The researchers compared neural signals elicited by works attributed to the two painters and analyzed whether the signals differentiated the artists.

headline: Can an interior’s geometry steer both your aesthetic judgment and brain response?
title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors.
note: Participants judged architectural interiors while undergoing imaging. The authors related measured brain responses to architectural properties and participants’ evaluations.

headline: Does your brain admire a designed garden differently from a natural landscape?
title: Neural correlates of appreciating natural landscape and landscape garden: Evidence from an fMRI study
note: The study compared fMRI activity during judgments about landscape gardens and natural landscapes and interpreted differences as distinct aesthetic processing.

headline: Does spiritual practice help you learn to control your own brain signal?
title: Ability to Gain Control Over One's Own Brain Activity and its Relation to Spiritual Practice: A Multimodal Imaging Study
note: The authors used a multimodal imaging design to examine whether participants’ success at regulating measured brain activity varied with spiritual practice.

headline: Does loving-kindness meditation change which brain regions fluctuate together?
title: BOLD signal and functional connectivity associated with loving kindness meditation
note: The authors compared fMRI activity and functional connectivity during loving-kindness meditation, using the contrasts to characterize a specific meditative state.

headline: Does years of meditation leave a structural signature of compassion?
title: Structural changes in socio-affective networks: Multi-modal MRI findings in long-term meditation practitioners
note: The authors compared MRI measures in long-term practitioners and comparison participants and interpreted differences in regions associated with social and affective processes.

headline: Can EEG tell where information flows during loving-kindness meditation?
title: Distinct Patterns of Directed Brain Connectivity in Focused Attention, Open Monitoring, and Loving Kindness Meditation: An Electroencephalographic Granger Causality Study with Long-term Meditators.
note: The authors used Granger-based statistics on EEG to compare estimated directionality across three meditation styles in experienced practitioners.

headline: Can a functional connectome fingerprint an experienced meditator?
title: Exploring the Embodied Mind: Functional Connectome Fingerprinting of Meditation Expertise
note: The researchers used connectivity patterns to assess meditation expertise and interpreted differences in pattern similarity as a signature of practice.

headline: Can compassion training change your brain’s response to someone suffering?
title: Effects of compassion training on brain responses to suffering others
note: The authors related between-condition changes in fMRI responses to suffering to the mental practice of compassion.

headline: Does prayer ease pain by lowering activity in a parietofrontal network?
title: Reduced Pain Sensation and Reduced BOLD Signal in Parietofrontal Networks during Religious Prayer.
note: The researchers compared reported pain and fMRI activity under prayer conditions. They interpreted paired decreases in those measures as a possible mechanism of prayer-related analgesia.

headline: Can brain–heart coupling tell whether you are in the zone while gaming?
title: Brain-Heart Interaction and the Experience of Flow While Playing a Video Game
note: The study recorded electrophysiology during video-game play and related brain–heart measures to reported flow.

headline: Can a game’s difficulty dial reveal the neural ingredients of being in the zone?
title: Neural contributions to flow experience during video game playing
note: The researchers varied gameplay conditions and interpreted between-condition neural differences in terms of the experience of flow.

headline: Do believers in the paranormal have weaker resting beta waves?
title: Paranormal believers show reduced resting EEG beta band oscillations and inhibitory control than skeptics
note: The authors compared resting EEG and inhibitory-control performance in believers and skeptics and linked group differences in beta oscillations to the proposed role of inhibition.

headline: Does your brain register a mistake even when you cannot make one?
title: Error monitoring when no errors are possible: Arbitrary free-choice decisions invoke error monitoring processes
note: The researchers recorded EEG during arbitrary choices and interpreted an error-monitoring response despite the absence of objectively wrong answers.

headline: Can an electrode distinguish free choices from instructed ones as a person plans an eye movement?
title: Decoding the neural dynamics of free choice in humans
note: The study used intracranial EEG in epilepsy patients to classify self-chosen versus instructed eye-movement trials and interpreted sustained high-gamma activity as an index of deliberation.

headline: Can a scan locate the feeling of being free to choose?
title: Brain correlates of subjective freedom of choice
note: The researchers compared reported freedom of choice with brain activity and interpreted the resulting contrasts as neural correlates of subjective freedom.

headline: Can brain stimulation make you less likely to ignore bad news about your future?
title: Selectively altering belief formation in the human brain
note: The authors altered prefrontal activity with stimulation and compared how participants updated beliefs after receiving favorable and unfavorable probabilities.

headline: Does one brain region help keep you optimistic despite bad news?
title: How unrealistic optimism is maintained in the face of reality
note: Participants revised estimates of their likelihood of life events after seeing population statistics. The authors related asymmetric revisions to fMRI responses and individual optimism.

headline: Do optimists’ brains resemble one another when they imagine the future?
title: Optimistic people are all alike: Shared neural representations supporting episodic future thinking among optimistic individuals
note: The authors used fMRI pattern similarity during future-event simulation and compared it across individuals with different optimism scores.

headline: Does your reward circuitry pay you for looking at something gruesome?
title: Choosing to view morbid information involves reward circuitry
note: Participants chose whether to view morbid information. The authors linked choices to fMRI activation in regions often studied in reward tasks.

headline: Can resting brain connectivity explain what you get curious about in daily life?
title: Curiosity and mesolimbic functional connectivity drive information seeking in real life
note: The authors linked connectivity in a reward-related circuit and measures of curiosity to reported information seeking outside the scanner.

headline: Can a brain scan tell when someone is reliving a breakup?
title: Hippocampus, amygdala, and insula activation in response to romantic relationship dissolution stimuli: A case-case-control fMRI study on emerging adult students.
note: The researchers compared responses to breakup-related material and interpreted group differences in hippocampal, amygdala and insular activity in terms of relationship dissolution.

headline: Does the brain revise its representation of a crush after friends weigh in?
title: The mentalizing network updates neural representations of romantic interest in response to social feedback
note: The study related brain patterns during judgments of romantic interest to social feedback and interpreted changes in the mentalizing network as updating the representation.

headline: Does the brain represent a loved one’s pain more like your own than a stranger’s?
title: Love hurts: an fMRI study.
note: Participants imagined painful events from the perspective of themselves, a partner or a stranger. The authors related right temporoparietal activity to closeness and interpreted the contrasts as overlap in representations of self and partner.

headline: Do you borrow other people’s taste in partners with your prefrontal cortex?
title: A Role of DLPFC in the Learning Process of Human Mate Copying
note: The study examined how learning other people’s evaluations changed attractiveness judgments and related the effect to dorsolateral prefrontal activity.

headline: Do brain responses to social feedback reveal how much you see your partner as yourself?
title: For better and worse: neural self-partner overlap during social feedback is associated with relationship satisfaction and depressive symptoms.
note: The authors quantified similarity between neural responses involving self and partner and related it to relationship satisfaction and depressive symptoms.

headline: Does your partner’s well-being show up in the way your brain thinks about them?
title: Theory-of-mind-related neural activity for one’s romantic partner predicts partner well-being
note: The researchers related neural activity while participants inferred their partner’s mental states to well-being measures reported by the partner.

headline: Does a dose of oxytocin quiet the brain’s response to baby faces?
title: Oxytocin reduces neural activation in response to infant faces in nulliparous young women
note: The researchers compared women given oxytocin or placebo and reported lower responses to infant faces in selected regions after oxytocin.

headline: Can a scan locate maternal love when a baby seeks its mother’s attention?
title: The functional neuroanatomy of maternal love: mother's response to infant's attachment behaviors
note: The authors scanned mothers viewing their infants’ attachment behavior and interpreted the pattern of responses in terms of maternal love.

headline: Does a baby’s smell register as cute in a brain scan?
title: The scent of cuteness—neural signatures of infant body odors
note: Across two fMRI studies, mothers and women without children smelled infant and postpubertal body odors. The authors interpreted stronger reward-related responses to infant odors as a counterpart to the effects of infant facial features.
