headline: Does romantic love recruit a mechanism for choosing a mate?
title: Romantic love: an fMRI study of a neural mechanism for mate choice
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to photographs of a loved person and comparison photographs and interpreted the results as evidence about human mate choice.

headline: Does a touch from your partner have a different brain signature from a stranger’s?
title: How the brain codes intimacy: The neurobiological substrates of romantic touch
note: The researchers compared responses to touch across relationship conditions and related these patterns to the subjective experience of romantic intimacy.

headline: Can a hormone amplify the brain’s response to the sights and smells of attraction?
title: Kisspeptin enhances brain responses to olfactory and visual cues of attraction in men
note: The study compared imaging responses to cues of attraction under kisspeptin and placebo and interpreted the contrasts as effects on attraction-related processing.

headline: Do brainwaves give away when a speed dater is accepted or rejected?
title: Neural correlates of acceptance and rejection in online speed dating: An electroencephalography study.
note: The researchers measured EEG while participants received acceptance or rejection feedback in an online speed-dating task and compared responses to the two outcomes.

headline: Do narcissistic men get a reward from looking at their own faces?
title: Self-viewing is associated with negative affect rather than reward in highly narcissistic men: an fMRI study
note: The researchers compared self-face fMRI responses by narcissism scores and interpreted group differences in terms of negative affect during self-viewing.

headline: Does looking at yourself tune face-processing brainwaves differently?
title: The ‘Narcissus Effect’: Top-down alpha-beta band modulation of face-related brain areas during self-face processing
note: The authors compared EEG responses to the self-face and other faces and interpreted band-specific effects as top-down modulation during self-recognition.

headline: Do people high in narcissistic traits respond less alike when they see someone else socially threatened?
title: Reduced social brain coupling to others' face threats in narcissism.
note: The authors compared between-viewer similarity in fMRI responses to others being socially threatened and related lower similarity in some regions to higher grandiose narcissism scores.

headline: Can online approval calm narcissists’ brain responses after rejection?
title: Social Media Approval Reduces Emotional Arousal for People High in Narcissism: Electrophysiological Evidence
note: The study used an exclusion task, a social media approval manipulation and an auditory EEG response. It related changes in the response to narcissism scores.

headline: Can you see narcissistic admiration and rivalry in the first brainwaves after a face appears?
title: Face Perception and Narcissism: Variations of Event-Related Potential Components (P1 & N170) with Admiration and Rivalry
note: The authors related two components of narcissism scores to early face-evoked ERP amplitudes.

headline: Does heavy phone and social media use show up in the resting brain?
title: Altered functional brain networks in problematic smartphone and social media use: resting-state fMRI study
note: The researchers grouped participants using problematic-use measures and compared their resting-state functional networks.

headline: Does a smartphone addiction score come with a brain anatomy signature?
title: Structural and functional correlates of smartphone addiction.
note: The authors compared MRI anatomy and resting activity across people with different levels of problematic phone use and discussed the differences as addiction correlates.

headline: Can you read poorer executive control in the connectedness of a heavy phone user’s brain?
title: Aberrant intrinsic neural network strength in individuals with “smartphone addiction”: An MRI data fusion study
note: The authors combined MRI signal measures in a data-fusion model and proposed a resting-network signature of insufficient executive control in problematic smartphone use.

headline: Does too much social networking have a distinctive brain morphology?
title: Brain anatomy alterations associated with Social Networking Site (SNS) addiction
note: The study related structural MRI measures to social networking addiction scores and interpreted the associations against findings from gambling and substance use.

headline: Does watching lots of short videos leave a mark on the resting brain?
title: Association between usage intensity of short video platforms and altered brain function: a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging study
note: The researchers related short-video use intensity to spontaneous fMRI activity and connectivity measures.

headline: Does a pathological gamer’s brain treat their avatar as part of the self?
title: Exploring the Neural Basis of Avatar Identification in Pathological Internet Gamers and of Self-Reflection in Pathological Social Network Users
note: The researchers compared patterns during self-reflection and avatar judgments in gaming and social networking groups and interpreted them in terms of identification.

headline: Can brain scans advise winemakers on the right alcohol level?
title: What can the brain teach us about winemaking? An fMRI study of alcohol level preferences
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to wines with different alcohol levels and interpreted differences as greater attentional exploration of flavors and aromas.

headline: Does just expecting alcohol change connections in the brain’s reward system?
title: Neural underpinnings of expecting alcohol: Placebo alcohol administration alters nucleus accumbens resting state functional connectivity
note: The researchers compared resting fMRI after placebo alcohol with comparison conditions and proposed reward-network connectivity as one route by which expectation contributes to intoxication.

headline: Does a Coke logo light up different regions in kids who drink soft drinks regularly?
title: Neural responsivity during soft drink intake, anticipation, and advertisement exposure in habitually consuming youth
note: The authors grouped youth by consumption and compared their responses to drink anticipation, intake and advertising, including Coke logos.

headline: Does a Fairtrade label make the same chocolate taste better to the brain?
title: Effects of social sustainability signaling on neural valuation signals and taste-experience of food products
note: The researchers varied sustainability labels and related taste and value ratings for chocolate to fMRI responses. They described the rating change as a taste placebo effect.

headline: Does putting an organic label on food boost a reward signal?
title: Organic labeling influences food valuation and choice
note: The authors compared labeled and unlabeled food options during scanning and related ventral striatal responses to everyday organic consumption.

headline: Does expecting to enjoy hot sauce change how the brain responds to the burn?
title: The expectations humans have of a pleasurable sensation asymmetrically shape neuronal responses and subjective experiences to hot sauce
note: The authors manipulated expectations before tasting hot sauce and compared subjective ratings and neural responses according to whether participants liked spicy food.

headline: Do people who eat spicy food often process the pleasure of capsaicin in a different region?
title: Differential neural correlates of oral capsaicin pleasantness in habitual and non-habitual spicy eaters.
note: The researchers compared habitual and nonhabitual spicy-food consumers and related neural responses to pleasantness ratings for capsaicin.

headline: Can a picture of chili peppers reveal a craving for extreme spice?
title: Extreme spicy food cravers displayed increased brain activity in response to pictures of foods containing chili peppers: an fMRI study
note: The researchers compared fMRI responses to food pictures in groups distinguished by reported spicy-food craving.

headline: Does chocolate feel more rewarding to the brain of a chocolate craver?
title: Enhanced affective brain representations of chocolate in cravers vs. non-cravers
note: The study compared brain responses to chocolate cues in self-described cravers and noncravers and interpreted the differences as enhanced affective representations.

headline: Can scanning a few people reveal what a much larger market will pick?
title: Neuroforecasting reveals generalizable components of choice
note: The researchers compared measures from individual participants with aggregate choices and inferred a component of valuation that generalizes across decision makers.

headline: Can your insula give away whether you trade stocks outside the lab?
title: Preferences and beliefs about financial risk taking mediate the association between anterior insula activation and self-reported real-life stock trading
note: In 157 working-age men, the authors related anterior insula activity during risky versus safe laboratory choices to self-reported active stock trading. They fit mediation models with financial risk preferences and beliefs.

headline: Can a scan show which anti-smoking message will change what a smoker does next?
title: Brain Activity in Self- and Value-Related Regions in Response to Online Antismoking Messages Predicts Behavior Change
note: Researchers related activity in self- and value-related brain regions during online messages to subsequent changes in smoking behavior.

headline: Can a teenager’s brain response to a food commercial forecast weight gain?
title: Individual Differences in Striatum Activity to Food Commercials Predict Weight Gain in Adolescents
note: The authors related adolescent striatal fMRI responses to food ads to subsequent weight change.

headline: Is the striatum where an investor decides to follow the herd?
title: Striatal BOLD Response Reflects the Impact of Herd Information on Financial Decisions
note: The authors compared responses to human and nonsocial choice information and related ventral striatal signals to how much the information changed a financial decision.

headline: Can your striatum tell which income inequality is fair?
title: Equity theory and fair inequality: a neuroeconomic study
note: The authors varied income distributions in an allocation task and related activity during evaluation to self-reported judgments of equity.

headline: Can a brain response to unequal payouts forecast depression scores?
title: Brain response patterns to economic inequity predict present and future depression indices
note: The authors related fMRI patterns in an economic inequity task to current and later depression measures and interpreted the results in terms of sensitivity to inequality.

headline: Does altruistic punishment have an EEG signature that varies with empathy?
title: The interplay between feedback-related negativity and individual differences in altruistic punishment: An EEG study.
note: The researchers related an EEG response to unfair offers and punishment behavior, comparing first- and third-party conditions and examining trait empathy.

headline: Does taking a loss change the neural price you will pay to enforce fairness?
title: Neural basis of increased costly norm enforcement under adversity
note: The authors fit a model of costly punishment across gain and loss conditions and interpreted the neural contrasts in terms of how people respond to adversity.

headline: Does the brain evaluate the same unfair offer differently when you can punish it?
title: Power to Punish Norm Violations Affects the Neural Processes of Fairness-Related Decision Making
note: The researchers compared responses across games that gave participants different powers to sanction and used fMRI contrasts to infer changes in the fairness decision process.

headline: Can fMRI separate how much an outsider cares about unfairness from how much they care about intent?
title: Computational Substrates of Social Norm Enforcement by Unaffected Third Parties
note: The authors modeled third-party sanctions using measures of inequity and intentionality and related these model components to activity in different regions.

headline: Can a brain scan see the conflict between good intentions and breaking the law?
title: When morality opposes the law: An fMRI investigation into punishment judgments for crimes with good intentions
note: Participants judged punishment for crimes described as having different motives. The authors interpreted fMRI contrasts in terms of moral and legal conflict.

headline: Can disrupting prefrontal activity change how blame turns into punishment?
title: From blame to punishment: Disrupting prefrontal cortex activity reveals norm enforcement mechanisms
note: The researchers used stimulation and criminal scenarios to compare blame assessments and punishment judgments and infer a role in translating one into the other.

headline: Can a scan separate the mental arithmetic of harm from criminal responsibility?
title: Parsing the Behavioral and Brain Mechanisms of Third-Party Punishment
note: The authors modeled punishment choices using descriptions that varied harm and responsibility and compared the associated fMRI signals.

headline: Which parts of the brain become active when a crime deserves a lighter sentence?
title: Neural circuits in the brain that are activated when mitigating criminal sentences
note: The researchers compared fMRI responses to criminal scenarios with different mitigating circumstances and interpreted contrasts in terms of sentence mitigation.

headline: Does suppressing the truth light up a basic deception circuit?
title: Brain activity during simulated deception: an event-related functional magnetic resonance study.
note: The authors compared fMRI signals during simulated truthful and deceptive responses and proposed that inhibition of truthful responses was part of a core deception circuit.

headline: Can a scan tell how good a liar you are?
title: Lying in the scanner: localized inhibition predicts lying skill.
note: The researchers related behavioral performance on a lying task to localized activation and interpreted the result as a neural predictor of lying skill.

headline: Can electrical patterns tell when a decision becomes dishonest?
title: The path of dishonesty: identification of mental processes with electrical neuroimaging
note: The authors used time-resolved EEG analysis to infer the sequence of mental processes during experimentally elicited honest and dishonest choices.

headline: Can a connectivity map predict how much you lie for money?
title: I lie, why don't you: Neural mechanisms of individual differences in self‐serving lying
note: The authors compared activation and functional coupling across individuals in a self-serving deception task and related those patterns to how often participants lied.

headline: Does self-control make honest people cheat and cheaters tell the truth?
title: Cognitive Control Promotes Either Honesty or Dishonesty, Depending on One's Moral Default
note: The researchers compared signals on a cognitive-control task with choices on a separate cheating task and interpreted opposite associations in terms of participants’ moral defaults.

headline: Does beating someone else change how your brain computes regret and whether you gamble again?
title: Social comparison modulates the neural responses to regret and subsequent risk-taking behavior
note: The authors compared outcomes against another person’s results and linked reward-region connectivity during the task to later risk-taking.

headline: Can the amygdala tell whether you blame yourself for a bad decision?
title: Amygdala involvement in self-blame regret
note: The authors manipulated responsibility for outcomes and related amygdala activity to objective and reported responsibility during regret.

headline: Does remembering guilt use different regions from imagining it?
title: 'Imagined guilt' vs 'recollected guilt': implications for fMRI
note: The researchers compared fMRI signals for recollected and imagined guilt and discussed whether the two inductions probe the same processes.

headline: Does moral disgust enlist the same brain machinery as physical revulsion?
title: The moral affiliations of disgust: a functional MRI study
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to different kinds of disgust and attributed parts of the contrast to automatic moral judgment.

headline: Can feeling physically gross change the neural processing of purity violations?
title: Effects of Core Disgust and Moral Disgust on Moral Judgment: An Event-Related Potential Study
note: The study primed different types of disgust, compared judgments across types of moral violation and used ERP differences to infer temporal stages.

headline: Does moral disgust build on physical disgust in the insula?
title: Functional Dissociation of the Posterior and Anterior Insula in Moral Disgust.
note: The authors compared posterior and anterior insular responses across kinds of disgust and interpreted the dissociation as evidence about how moral disgust is constructed.

headline: Does the brain process immoral behavior before physical disgust?
title: Temporal Dynamics of Disgust and Morality: An Event-Related Potential Study
note: The researchers compared the timing of event-related potentials for disgust and moral scenarios and used timing differences to infer which evaluations arise earlier.

headline: Does damage to one prefrontal area make other people less disgusting?
title: Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex reduces interpersonal disgust
note: The authors compared disgust ratings across lesion and control groups and proposed a selective causal role for the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in interpersonal disgust.

headline: Does your brain silently stamp moral violations as bad while you read?
title: Online processing of moral transgressions: ERP evidence for spontaneous evaluation
note: The authors compared EEG responses to morally acceptable and unacceptable words and interpreted a later positivity as spontaneous good–bad categorization.

headline: Does understanding envy and gloating use a shared mindreading network?
title: The green-eyed monster and malicious joy: the neuroanatomical bases of envy and gloating (schadenfreude)
note: The authors used neuroanatomical and behavioral measures to link the ability to understand competitive emotions to perspective-taking and mentalizing.

headline: Can your brain reveal when you are projecting your envy onto somebody else?
title: Projecting my envy onto you: neurocognitive mechanisms of an offline emotional egocentricity bias.
note: The researchers compared emotion judgments and neural signals to test whether personal envy biased inferences about another person’s feelings.

headline: Does malicious envy make the brain enjoy a rival’s loss on a different timetable?
title: ERP Effects of Malicious Envy on Schadenfreude in Gain and Loss Frames
note: The authors varied gain and loss framing, comparing EEG responses to another person’s misfortune after inducing envy.

headline: Can fMRI show how you learn which charity does more with your money?
title: Learn how to be effective: neural and computational insights into charity efficiency learning
note: The researchers modeled how participants updated expected charity efficiency and compared the related brain responses with those from a monetary reward-learning task.

headline: Can EEG predict how much you will donate on the next trial?
title: Multivariate pattern analysis of electroencephalography data reveals information predictive of charitable giving
note: The study used electrical responses to emotional images and charity cues to model the amount donated on individual decisions.

headline: Can a brainwave tell whether you care more about charity’s winnings than your own?
title: Altruistic traits are predicted by neural responses to monetary outcomes for self vs charity
note: The authors compared ERP responses to payouts for self versus charity and related differences to altruism measures.

headline: Does cortical thickness tell how much a child will give away?
title: Neuroanatomical correlates of donating behavior in middle childhood
note: The authors related structural MRI measurements to giving in a childhood donation task and contrasted the anatomical findings with resting connectivity results.

headline: Does the brain’s opioid system explain why you pay to help somebody else?
title: Endogenous opioid receptor system mediates costly altruism in the human brain
note: The authors combined an opioid-receptor PET measure with fMRI responses during helping and interpreted the association as modulation of costly altruism.

headline: Does compulsory giving look different on EEG from giving by choice?
title: Neural Responses to Mandatory and Voluntary Donation Impact Charitable Giving Decisions: An Event-Related Potentials Study
note: The researchers compared ERP signals and donation amounts across mandatory and voluntary giving conditions.

headline: Can the shape of your brain tell how quickly you spot a high-status person?
title: Neuroanatomical Markers of Social Hierarchy Recognition in Humans: A Combined ERP/MRI Study
note: The study combined anatomical MRI and event-related potentials during hierarchy recognition and related individual differences to brain morphology.

headline: Does your brain care more whether a higher-status person takes your advice?
title: The impact of social hierarchies on neural response to feedback evaluations after advice giving
note: The authors assigned ranks using a dot-estimation task and recorded advisers’ EEG as they learned whether higher- or lower-ranked participants accepted their advice and whether it was correct.

headline: Does an accent that doesn’t match a face trigger an EEG surprise signal?
title: When appearance does not match accent: neural correlates of ethnicity-related expectancy violations
note: The authors varied apparent ethnicity and accent together and interpreted differences in brain responses as violations of expectations about the speaker.

headline: Does the face you see change how efficiently your brain processes an accent?
title: The neural processing of foreign-accented speech and its relationship to listener bias
note: The researchers paired speech with faces and related aspects of EEG speech tracking to implicit bias and perceived foreignness.

headline: Can a scan tell when a race or gender stereotype is activated or suppressed?
title: Neural correlates of automatic beliefs about gender and race
note: The authors compared brain responses during stereotype-related judgments and inferred separate prefrontal contributions to stereotype activation and inhibition.

headline: Can EEG reveal a preference for people who talk like you?
title: A Neural Marker for Social Bias Toward In-group Accents
note: The researchers compared responses to own-group and other accents and interpreted a group-sensitive EEG signal as a marker of accent bias.

headline: Does an individualist have a different neural self from a collectivist?
title: Neural basis of individualistic and collectivistic views of self
note: The authors compared functional activation during self-related judgments and used the differences to interpret individualistic and collectivistic views of self.

headline: Does growing up in a different culture change the size of brain regions?
title: Culture-Related and Individual Differences in Regional Brain Volumes: A Cross-Cultural Voxel-Based Morphometry Study
note: The researchers compared voxel-based MRI volume measures across cultural groups and related the differences to individual characteristics and possible cultural influences.

headline: Can a cultural cue change how your brain represents who you are?
title: Dynamic cultural influences on neural representations of the self
note: The researchers manipulated cultural framing and compared brain responses to judgments about the self, interpreting variation as a neural basis for acculturation.

headline: Does cultural background change which regions take the lead when you reflect on yourself?
title: Sociocultural patterning of neural activity during self-reflection
note: The authors related self-construal and cultural context to activity during self-reflection, inferring different weights for regions in a social-cognition network.

headline: Can an individualist prime change both your EEG and how friendly you act?
title: Effect of Cultural Priming on Social Behavior and EEG Correlates of Self-Processing
note: The researchers compared EEG patterns and a social-interaction task after primes for individualistic or other mindsets.

headline: Can your idea of yourself change the way the brain sorts the forest from the trees?
title: Self-Orientation Modulates the Neural Correlates of Global and Local Processing
note: The authors related self-orientation measures to neural responses during global and local visual judgments, interpreting the effects in terms of attention and conflict.

headline: Does looking at someone of another race in pain mute the observer’s cingulate signal?
title: Do you feel my pain? Racial group membership modulates empathic neural responses
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to same- and other-race faces undergoing painful stimulation and interpreted the contrast as an in-group empathy bias.

headline: Does seeing a needle prick dark or light skin change your EEG response?
title: Racial bias in empathy: Do we process dark- and fair-colored hands in pain differently? An EEG study
note: The authors compared ERPs while viewers saw hands of different skin colors receiving painful or nonpainful stimulation and related responses to implicit attitudes.

headline: Can beta waves reveal whose pain you feel more strongly?
title: Beta oscillations reveal ethnicity ingroup bias in sensorimotor resonance to pain of others
note: The researchers compared oscillatory activity during observation of people of different ethnic groups in painful conditions and interpreted beta differences as sensorimotor resonance.

headline: Can asking someone to focus on another person’s pain shrink a neural in-group bias?
title: Task modulations of racial bias in neural responses to others' suffering
note: The authors varied task instructions while participants viewed pain expressions and compared race-related fMRI contrasts across those instructions.

headline: Does how strongly you identify with your race change resting-network regions’ responses to faces?
title: Racial identification modulates default network activity for same and other races
note: The study related strength of racial identification to activity in default-network areas during judgments involving same- and other-race individuals.

headline: Can fMRI distinguish outright dehumanization from simple dislike?
title: Denying humanity: The distinct neural correlates of blatant dehumanization.
note: The authors asked participants to rate groups, modeled dehumanization and dislike separately and reported different neural correlates for the two judgments.

headline: Does being told why someone became homeless change which part of the brain evaluates them?
title: Does context matter in evaluations of stigmatized individuals? An fMRI study
note: The researchers varied descriptions of responsibility for homelessness and interpreted resulting fMRI contrasts in terms of affective and social evaluation.

headline: Can petting a dog put your brain into a relaxed but focused state?
title: Brain and heart activity during interactions with pet dogs: A portable electroencephalogram and heart rate variability study
note: The authors compared portable EEG and heart-rate measures across interactions with pet dogs and interpreted spectral changes as markers of relaxation and attention.

headline: Can a dog’s brain give away jealousy when its caregiver greets another dog?
title: Neural Responses of Pet Dogs Witnessing Their Caregiver's Positive Interactions with a Conspecific: An fMRI Study
note: The researchers scanned dogs observing their caregiver interact with another dog and interpreted activity differences as arousal and valence in a possible threat to the bond.

headline: Can EEG tell a real dog from a replica dog in a person’s lap?
title: Neural signature of human-dog interactions: EEG correlates from comparisons with plant and replica dog in a within-subject, cross-over randomized trial
note: The authors compared neural signals across interactions with a real dog, a replica and a plant and interpreted differences as evidence of social and emotional salience.

headline: Does your dog’s brain value your praise more because it comes from you?
title: Social relationship-dependent neural response to speech in dogs
note: The researchers compared canine brain responses to speech using the dog’s owner and other speakers and linked reward-area differences to attachment.

headline: Does getting to know a robot change the brain’s response to its pain?
title: A neurocognitive investigation of the impact of socializing with a robot on empathy for pain
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers compared neural and behavioral responses to a robot’s apparent pain across prior-interaction conditions.

headline: Do people’s brains empathize with a humanoid robot the way they do with a person?
title: Do we empathize humanoid robots and humans in the same way? Behavioral and multimodal brain imaging investigations.
note: The authors compared behavioral and imaging measures across human and robotic targets and used similarities and differences to infer kinds of empathy.

headline: Does a robot’s emotional face recruit the same regions as a person’s?
title: Brain response to a humanoid robot in areas implicated in the perception of human emotional gestures
note: The authors showed robotic and human emotional expressions and varied what viewers attended to. They interpreted changes in inferior frontal activity in terms of motor resonance.

headline: Do brainwaves flag an unfair split when your partner is a robot?
title: Neural correlates of inequity perception in human-robot relationships: An ERP study of solo and joint experiences.
note: The authors compared event-related potentials during unequal outcomes across solo and joint human–robot conditions.

headline: Can brain scans tell vegetarians from omnivores by how they react to suffering?
title: The brain functional networks associated to human and animal suffering differ among omnivores, vegetarians and vegans.
note: The authors compared brain activity across diet groups viewing human and animal suffering and interpreted differential responses in terms of empathy.

headline: Does the brain respond to harm to a forest the way it responds to harm to a person?
title: Overlapping neural response to the pain or harm of people, animals, and nature.
note: The study compared responses to harm targeting people, animals or nature and interpreted shared fMRI activity as evidence of a common response.

headline: Does becoming aware that you are dreaming have a brainwave signature?
title: Electrophysiological Correlates of Lucid Dreaming: Sensor and Source Level Signatures
note: The researchers compared lucid and nonlucid sleep in EEG and used frequency and source estimates to infer candidate mechanisms of lucid awareness.

headline: Does dreaming lucidly more often go with a different mix of gray and white matter?
title: Lucid Dreaming Frequency Associated With Grey–White Matter Networks: An Exploratory Multimodal MRI Study
note: The authors linked clusters of structural MRI features to reported lucid-dream frequency and interpreted the clusters through self-awareness and simulation.

headline: Can a patch at the back of the brain tell whether someone is dreaming?
title: The neural correlates of dreaming.
note: The researchers used EEG around awakenings to relate local spectral activity to whether participants reported dream experiences.

headline: Can EEG tell when dreaming has already begun before REM sleep?
title: EEG Predictors of Dreaming Outside of REM Sleep
note: The authors related reports after awakenings from non-REM sleep to EEG slowing and the appearance of larger slow oscillations.

headline: Does an immersive dream make sleep feel deeper than its physiology suggests?
title: Immersive NREM2 dreaming preserves subjective sleep depth against declining sleep pressure
note: The authors compared dream reports with perceived sleep depth and proposed that immersive non-REM dreaming buffers the decline in perceived depth.

headline: Does one corner of the default network imagine the scene while another decides if it sounds appealing?
title: The Ventral and Dorsal Default Mode Networks Are Dissociably Modulated by the Vividness and Valence of Imagined Events
note: The researchers related simulated events’ rated vividness and valence to distinct default-network subdivisions and interpreted the contrast as construction versus evaluation.

headline: Can a resting scan explain why you remember lots of dreams independently of how much REM sleep you get?
title: Dissociated resting-state functional networks between the dream recall frequency and REM sleep percentage
note: The authors separately related functional connectivity to dream recall frequency and percentage of REM sleep.

headline: Can an electrode bring back the feeling that you’ve dreamed this before?
title: Déjà-rêvé: Prior dreams induced by direct electrical brain stimulation
note: The authors classified dream-related experiences reported during direct brain stimulation and examined their anatomical distribution.

headline: Do brainwaves before you wake up predict whether you will remember a dream?
title: Recalling and forgetting dreams: theta and alpha oscillations during sleep predict subsequent dream recall
note: The authors compared sleep EEG before awakenings with later dream recall and interpreted frequency-specific effects in relation to episodic memory.

headline: Does yesterday’s audiobook replay in both your dreams and measured brain activity?
title: Pre-sleep experiences shape neural activity and dream content in the sleeping brain
note: The authors compared neural patterns during sleep with those measured around a presleep narrative and related reinstatement to whether dream reports incorporated it.

headline: Does connectivity right after waking explain why some people remember their dreams?
title: Brain functional connectivity upon awakening from sleep predicts interindividual differences in dream recall frequency
note: The researchers related fMRI coupling around awakening to habitual dream recall and proposed a short-term maintenance mechanism.

headline: Does mentally traveling through time use a different brain network from mentally traveling through space?
title: Time Is Not Space: Core Computations and Domain-Specific Networks for Mental Travels
note: The researchers compared neural responses across imagined movements in time and space and attributed the dissociation to distinct mental navigation systems.

headline: Can imagining yourself in a different political camp recruit a brain network for mental time travel?
title: Travelling beyond time: shared brain system for self-projection in the temporal, political and moral domains
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: Twenty-eight participants made judgments from their actual or imagined political, moral or temporal positions. The authors inferred a shared self-projection system from overlapping fMRI activity.

headline: Can a scan pick out who is suggestible even before anyone hypnotizes them?
title: What makes your brain suggestible? Hypnotizability is associated with differential brain activity during attention outside hypnosis.
note: The researchers related hypnotizability scores to neural responses during attention tasks outside hypnosis and interpreted network differences as cognitive flexibility.

headline: Does the resting brain give away how easily someone can be hypnotized?
title: Functional Brain Basis of Hypnotizability
note: The authors compared MRI connectivity across levels of hypnotizability and proposed that coupling between prefrontal and cingulate areas might underlie the trait.

headline: Does hypnosis uncouple noticing a conflict from acting on it?
title: Hypnosis decouples cognitive control from conflict monitoring processes of the frontal lobe
note: The authors measured brain activity during an attention task in hypnotic and comparison conditions and interpreted the response pattern as separation of control and monitoring.

headline: Does a hypnotized person’s brain hold a limb still by monitoring itself better?
title: The brain under self-control: modulation of inhibitory and monitoring cortical networks during hypnotic paralysis.
note: The authors contrasted suggested paralysis with control conditions and used activity patterns to distinguish self-monitoring from direct inhibition.

headline: Can a chemical measurement in one cingulate region tell how hypnotizable you are?
title: Association between Anterior Cingulate Neurochemical Concentration and Individual Differences in Hypnotizability
note: The authors related spectroscopy measurements in the anterior cingulate cortex to individual hypnotizability scores.

headline: Does frequent déjà vu leave signatures of familiarity without recollection in two brain areas?
title: Abnormal rsFC and GMV changes in parahippocampal and DLPFC for high Déjà vu experienced subjects
note: The authors grouped people by reported déjà vu and compared resting connectivity and gray-matter volume, interpreting differences through familiarity and context monitoring.

headline: Do people who get déjà vu have different hippocampal subfields?
title: Hippocampal involvement in nonpathological déjà vu: Subfield vulnerability rather than temporal lobe epilepsy equivalent
note: The researchers compared hippocampal measures with reported nonpathological déjà vu and interpreted a regional pattern in terms of selective vulnerability.

headline: Can slow oscillations in the resting brain explain that false feeling of familiarity?
title: Insights into déjà vu: Associations between the frequency of experience and amplitudes of low-frequency oscillations in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging.
note: The authors related resting fMRI fluctuation amplitudes to déjà vu frequency and proposed a disruption in cortico-subcortical communication.

headline: Which sense gives nostalgia the strongest brainwave response?
title: Harmonizing the past: EEG-based brain network unveil modality-specific mechanisms of nostalgia
note: The authors compared EEG during nostalgic experiences prompted through different sensory channels and examined variation in alpha activity.

headline: Does a nostalgic song change brain connections at different frequencies for different kinds of memory?
title: EEG-based functional connectivity uncovers frequency-specific brain network alterations induced by nostalgic music
note: The authors estimated EEG connectivity during nostalgic music and assigned different frequency changes to memory retrieval, emotion and visual recall.

headline: Does an old song start your autobiographical memory network without asking?
title: The Neural Architecture of Music-Evoked Autobiographical Memories
note: The authors scanned listeners hearing popular music and related activity to the autobiographical memories the songs elicited.

headline: Does zoning out during a boring film show up in the default network?
title: Boredom, sustained attention and the default mode network
note: The study compared fMRI connectivity during rest, sustained attention and videos designed to induce boredom or interest. The authors interpreted an insula–default network pattern as a sign of failure to stay engaged.

headline: Can a resting scan reveal which people feel lonely?
title: Brain activity and functional connectivity patterns associated with loneliness: A resting-state fMRI study.
note: The authors compared regional activity and functional connectivity with individual loneliness scores and proposed candidate networks for follow-up intervention research.

headline: Is being easily bored a sign of a more flexible brain network?
title: Bored out of my mind: Integrated and flexible brain networks define trait boredom.
note: The researchers related questionnaire scores for boredom proneness to measures of network integration and changing topology.

headline: Can a scan reveal perceived isolation in the default network?
title: The default network of the human brain is associated with perceived social isolation
note: The authors related reported loneliness to default-network anatomy and connectivity measures in a population imaging sample.

headline: Which parts of the hippocampus covary differently with the default network in lonely people?
title: Loneliness is linked to specific subregional alterations in hippocampus-default network covariation
note: The researchers analyzed structural covariation in a large imaging dataset, comparing patterns across loneliness status.

headline: How accurately can resting brain connections estimate someone’s loneliness?
title: Connectome-based individualized prediction of loneliness
note: The authors fit a connectome-based model to loneliness scores and discussed use of individual predictions in future research.

headline: Do you automatically give the most connected person in a new social network more space in your brain?
title: Neural encoding of novel social networks: evidence that perceivers prioritize others’ centrality
note: The authors trained people on unfamiliar social networks and tested whether fMRI patterns represented others’ network centrality.

headline: Do popular people’s brains respond more alike than everyone else’s?
title: In-degree centrality in a social network is linked to coordinated neural activity
note: The authors compared neural similarity during shared stimuli and related it to how often others in the social network named a person.

headline: Do school friends have matching social-brain anatomy?
title: The Anatomy of Friendship: Neuroanatomic Homophily of the Social Brain among Classroom Friends
note: The authors compared structural measurements in mutual classroom friends with those of other peer pairs and interpreted the similarity as anatomical homophily.

headline: Can your brain’s changing connectivity during a conversation give away the shape of your social network?
title: Brain connectivity dynamics during social interaction reflect social network structure
note: The researchers related dynamic connectivity in a social-interaction task to social network characteristics outside the task.

headline: Can the scan you get while being left out predict whether you will conform later?
title: Global brain dynamics during social exclusion predict subsequent behavioral conformity
note: The authors related global features of fMRI dynamics during exclusion to later changes in behavior under social influence.

headline: Does seeing what other people find attractive change how the brain later represents a face?
title: Social conformity updates the neural representation of facial attractiveness
note: The study gave participants group attractiveness ratings and used EEG pattern similarity during later face viewing to assess whether they had internalized those ratings.

headline: Do creative groups show more brain synchrony when they choose their own leaders?
title: Letting leaders spontaneously emerge yields better creative outcomes and higher leader-follower interbrain synchrony during creative group communication
note: The researchers compared appointed and spontaneously emerging leaders on group creativity scores and leader–follower coupling measured with fNIRS.

headline: Can student and teacher brainwaves tell which classroom interaction will help a lesson stick?
title: Brain-to-Brain Synchrony and Learning Outcomes Vary by Student-Teacher Dynamics: Evidence from a Real-world Classroom Electroencephalography Study
note: The authors related classroom EEG synchrony to interaction patterns and learning outcomes.

headline: Can synchrony between a teacher and student give away whether the student learned something?
title: Teacher-student neural coupling during teaching and learning
note: The authors measured brain signals during instruction and related teacher–learner coupling to test performance.

headline: Can synchronized teacher and student brains forecast changes in grades from one semester to the next?
title: Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms
note: The researchers estimated interbrain coupling in classrooms and related it to changes in academic performance across semesters.

headline: Does laughing together bond people by synchronizing their brains?
title: In sync through laughter? An fNIRS hyperscanning study on neural synchrony and social connection
note: The authors related fNIRS synchrony during shared laughter to measures of social connection.

headline: Can a connectivity model tell how creative a person is?
title: Robust prediction of individual creative ability from brain functional connectivity
note: The authors used task fMRI connectivity patterns to predict scores on measures of creative idea production and assessed the model in additional samples.

headline: Can disrupting the default network make your ideas less original?
title: Default mode network electrophysiological dynamics and causal role in creative thinking
note: The researchers used intracranial recordings and stimulation during creative thinking and compared originality under different conditions.

headline: Are creative minds better at switching between spontaneous and controlled brain networks?
title: Dynamic switching between brain networks predicts creative ability
note: The authors related dynamic switching measures from several imaging datasets to individual creative ability.

headline: Does being open to new experiences make your default network more efficient?
title: Personality and complex brain networks: The role of openness to experience in default network efficiency
note: The researchers used a graph-based efficiency measure of resting connectivity and related it to questionnaire scores for openness.

headline: Can spontaneous brainwaves distinguish different kinds of narcissism?
title: Decoding the Narcissistic Brain
note: The authors used resting neural oscillations to predict questionnaire measures of different dimensions of narcissism.

headline: Can a moral dilemma reveal wisdom in a brain scan?
title: Individual differences in level of wisdom are associated with brain activation during a moral decision‐making task
note: The authors related scores on a wisdom measure to fMRI activation during a moral decision task.

headline: Do people prone to gratitude or pride have more gray matter in different places?
title: Individual differences in posterior cortical volume correlate with proneness to pride and gratitude
note: The researchers related cortical volume measures to individual differences in self-reported proneness to the two emotions.

headline: Does having a purpose in life show up in white-matter measurements?
title: Purpose in life as a resilience factor for brain health: diffusion MRI findings from the Midlife in the U.S. study
note: The researchers related self-reported purpose to diffusion MRI in a midlife and older-adult sample and discussed possible implications for healthy brain aging.

headline: Can a functional connectome predict your Big Five personality scores?
title: Robust prediction of individual personality from brain functional connectome
note: The researchers trained prediction models on connectivity data and assessed their ability to estimate ratings for individual personality dimensions.

headline: Does a brain structure measure explain why conscientious students get better grades?
title: Brain structure links trait conscientiousness to academic performance.
note: The authors measured brain anatomy, conscientiousness and academic performance and used their associations to propose a neural link between the trait and grades.

headline: Can a structural scan estimate how badly you want a definite answer?
title: Multivariate morphological brain signatures enable individualized prediction of dispositional need for closure
note: The authors used multiple MRI morphology measures to predict individual scores for dispositional need for closure.

headline: Does being a morning or evening person change the brain response to risky choices?
title: The effect of chronotype in risky decision making: An ERP study
note: The researchers compared EEG responses during a risk task for groups defined by morningness and eveningness scores.

headline: Does being a night owl show up in gray-matter volume?
title: Diurnal Preference and Grey Matter Volume in a Large Population of Older Adults: Data from the UK Biobank
note: The authors related reported diurnal preference to gray-matter measures from older UK Biobank participants.

headline: Can meditating on gratitude change how brain and heart signals track each other?
title: Effects of gratitude meditation on neural network functional connectivity and brain-heart coupling
note: The study compared gratitude meditation with another mental exercise and used changes in connectivity and heart-related measurements to infer differences in emotional regulation.

headline: Can the brain calculate gratitude from what a favor costs the giver and what you gain?
title: Decomposing Gratitude: Representation and Integration of Cognitive Antecedents of Gratitude in the Brain
note: The authors modeled gratitude ratings using the costs and benefits of favors and mapped fitted components and their integration to fMRI activity.

headline: Can practicing gratitude teach the brain pure altruism?
title: The Cultivation of Pure Altruism via Gratitude: A Functional MRI Study of Change with Gratitude Practice
note: The researchers compared fMRI responses to gains for oneself versus a charity after a gratitude exercise and interpreted changes in valuation activity as increased altruism.

headline: Can MEG reveal the moment a meditator’s sense of self fades?
title: Mindfulness-induced selflessness: a MEG neurophenomenological study
note: The authors compared oscillatory patterns during meditation conditions intended to produce different experiences of self.

headline: Can a scan distinguish feeling grateful for a favor from feeling indebted?
title: The psychological, computational, and neural foundations of indebtedness
note: The authors modeled indebtedness across favor scenarios and used imaging responses to link reported feelings and component processes to brain activity.

headline: Do people who get no pleasure from music have weaker hearing-to-reward connections?
title: Neural correlates of specific musical anhedonia
note: The researchers compared groups varying in music reward sensitivity and linked low enjoyment to functional interactions between auditory cortex and subcortical reward areas.

headline: Does music leave some people cold because of the way their white matter is organized?
title: White Matter Correlates of Musical Anhedonia: Implications for Evolution of Music
note: The authors compared diffusion-based tract measures with musical anhedonia and used the associations to inform an evolutionary account of music.

headline: Can white matter explain why a piece of music is a reward for one person and background noise for another?
title: White Matter Microstructure Reflects Individual Differences in Music Reward Sensitivity
note: The researchers related diffusion MRI estimates to a measure of music reward sensitivity and interpreted the findings in terms of communication between reward and cortical areas.

headline: Do ASMR sounds connect the brain differently than classical music?
title: Differences in brain functional connectivity between autonomous sensory meridian response and classical music
note: The authors compared selected functional connections during trigger sounds and classical music and interpreted the differences in terms of self-related processing and sensory integration.

headline: Do an acupuncturist’s brain signals align with a patient’s during needling?
title: The increased inter-brain neural synchronization in prefrontal cortex between simulated patient and acupuncturist during acupuncture stimulation: Evidence from functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning
note: The researchers used paired fNIRS during an acupuncture simulation and interpreted increased prefrontal synchrony as a feature of practitioner–recipient interaction.

headline: Do real and imagined acupuncture relieve pain through different brain responses?
title: Analgesic Effects Evoked by Real and Imagined Acupuncture: A Neuroimaging Study
note: The authors contrasted needling with guided imagery, comparing pain ratings and activation patterns elicited by the two procedures.

headline: Can a brain connectivity model explain how gut bacteria affect cognition?
title: Brain Network Topology and Structural-Functional Connectivity Coupling Mediate the Association Between Gut Microbiota and Cognition
note: The authors related microbiome profiles, MRI network measures and cognitive performance using statistical mediation.

headline: Can gut microbial types give away how good your memory is via the brain?
title: Microbial enterotype is linked to episodic and working memories via brain function in the parietal and occipital cortices.
note: The researchers associated gut microbial groups with memory scores and modeled parietal and occipital functional signals as intermediates.

headline: Does a gut microbiome influence cognition by making the brain look older?
title: Brain age mediates gut microbiome dysbiosis-related cognition in older adults
note: The study related microbiome differences to cognitive performance and fitted MRI-derived brain age as a statistical mediator.

headline: Can your gut bacteria leave a distributed signature on resting brain connectivity?
title: Multivariate associative patterns between the gut microbiota and large-scale brain network connectivity
note: The authors analyzed multivariate associations between microbial abundance and connectivity across large-scale brain networks in healthy participants.

headline: Does the menstrual cycle make whole-brain activity more turbulent?
title: The Menstrual Cycle Modulates Whole-Brain Turbulent Dynamics.
note: The authors applied turbulence measures to repeated imaging across the cycle and linked the resulting estimates to cycle phase and ovarian hormone measurements.

headline: Is there a time of the menstrual cycle when the brain applies the brakes to impulsivity?
title: Neural Basis of Increased Cognitive Control of Impulsivity During the Mid-Luteal Phase Relative to the Late Follicular Phase of the Menstrual Cycle
note: The study compared control-task behavior and frontostriatal imaging responses across two phases and interpreted them in relation to cyclical changes in impulsivity.

headline: Can a month of brain scans show neural networks reorganizing with ovarian hormones?
title: Dynamic community detection reveals transient reorganization of functional brain networks across a female menstrual cycle
note: The authors used community detection on dense longitudinal imaging across a menstrual cycle and related changes in network assignment to measured hormone fluctuations.

headline: Do soldiers and civilians have different brain signatures when refusing to obey for someone else’s benefit?
title: Neuro-cognitive specificities in prosocial disobedience: A comparative fMRI study of civilian and military populations
note: The authors compared military and civilian participants on a prosocial disobedience task and interpreted between-group brain patterns in light of institutional roles.

headline: Can an MRI signal tell who will resist a harmful order?
title: When the brain says “No!”: An MRI study on the neural correlates of resistance to immoral orders
note: The authors related MRI measures to the frequency of refusing instructions in an experimental prosocial disobedience task.

headline: Can the complexity of brain signals reveal who is vulnerable to misinformation?
title: Exploring the neurophysiological basis of misinformation: A behavioral and neural complexity analysis
note: The authors compared behavioral judgments and neural complexity measures in a misinformation task and discussed the potential for identifying susceptibility.

headline: Can a brain scan explain why people abuse power for personal gain?
title: Neural basis of corruption in power-holders
note: Participants acting as power-holders in a game decided whether to take a bribe. The researchers fit a decision model and attributed activity in separate regions to cooperating with a dishonest briber and to harming a third party.

headline: Do men and women use different brain modules to imagine a partner cheating?
title: Men and women show distinct brain activations during imagery of sexual and emotional infidelity
note: The researchers compared fMRI during imagined sexual and emotional infidelity and interpreted sex-by-scenario contrasts as evidence for different neuropsychological modules.

headline: Can the dog’s caudate tell whether it would choose praise over food?
title: Awake canine fMRI predicts dogs' preference for praise vs food
note: Fifteen awake dogs were scanned while cues signaled praise, food or neither. The authors related caudate responses to whether each dog later chose its owner or food in a Y-maze.

headline: Can an eight-week tutoring gain be forecast from a child’s brain scan?
title: Neural predictors of individual differences in response to math tutoring in primary-grade school children
note: Twenty-four third graders were scanned before eight weeks of one-to-one tutoring. The authors related initial hippocampal volume and connectivity to differences in improvement on an arithmetic task.

headline: Does white matter reveal how likely you are to procrastinate?
title: Neural markers of procrastination in white matter microstructures and networks.
note: The authors related diffusion MRI to questionnaire-rated procrastination across three samples totaling 901 people. They used the third sample to build models predicting questionnaire scores.

headline: Can a novel change your brain connections for several days after you finish reading?
title: Short- and long-term effects of a novel on connectivity in the brain
note: The authors collected daily resting fMRI across a period of reading and reported changes persisting after the last session, interpreting somatosensory results through embodied semantics.

headline: Does a full moon alter both human sleep and how readily the cortex responds?
title: Human sleep and cortical reactivity are influenced by lunar phase
note: The authors retrospectively grouped sleep data from 47 volunteers by lunar phase. They reported shorter sleep and greater cortical responses to environmental stimuli around the full moon.

headline: Do professional comedians have a larger funny bone somewhere in the brain?
title: Mapping the 'funny bone': neuroanatomical correlates of humor creativity in professional comedians.
note: The authors compared brain anatomy and humor creativity in professional comedians and other participants and interpreted structural differences alongside prior improvisation results.

headline: Can expecting caffeine trigger a dopamine response before you get any caffeine?
title: Expectation of caffeine induces dopaminergic responses in humans
note: The authors used PET to compare dopamine-related measures under expectations of caffeine and interpreted the results as a pharmacological placebo response.

headline: Can a brain scan help identify people willing to pursue someone else’s partner?
title: The neural basis of individual differences in mate poaching
note: Men rated how much they wanted a relationship with each woman pictured, whose stated relationship status varied. The authors linked orbitofrontal responses to differences in these ratings.

headline: Can an hour walking through a forest change a hippocampal MRI measurement?
title: Can a nature walk change your brain? Investigating hippocampal brain plasticity after one hour in a forest.
note: Sixty participants took an hour-long forest or city walk. The reported increase in MRI-estimated volume of one hippocampal subfield after the forest walk did not survive the authors’ Bonferroni correction.

headline: Can brain synchrony between a violinist and listeners predict how popular the performance will be?
title: The averaged inter-brain coherence between the audience and a violinist predicts the popularity of violin performance
note: Sixteen listeners watched prerecorded clips of the violinist playing 12 pieces. The authors related coherence between performer and listener fNIRS signals to the listeners’ evaluations of the pieces.

headline: Can your friends’ brain scans reproduce the pattern of how you see yourself?
title: The neural representation of self is recapitulated in the brains of friends: A round-robin fMRI study
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors used a round-robin fMRI design to compare neural patterns for self-judgments with those elicited when friends judged the same person.

headline: Why does one person’s suffering show up more strongly in a brain scan than a crowd’s?
title: Brain imaging evidence for why we are numbed by numbers
note: The authors contrasted fMRI responses to events involving one person or many and proposed a medial prefrontal marker for reduced engagement with large-scale suffering.

headline: Does a Catholic’s brain react differently to a moral dilemma that pits helping against killing?
title: Roman Catholic beliefs produce characteristic neural responses to moral dilemmas.
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to dilemmas across belief groups and interpreted the contrasts in terms of conflict between religious injunctions.

headline: Can a quantum annealing algorithm find brain signals that track university entrance exam scores?
title: Investigating the relationship between CSAT scores and prefrontal fNIRS signals during cognitive tasks using a quantum annealing algorithm
note: The authors used a feature-selection algorithm on prefrontal fNIRS signals collected during cognitive tasks and related the selected features to Korean CSAT scores.

headline: Does attachment style change the brain response to being left out?
title: Do neural responses to rejection depend on attachment style? An fMRI study
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to social exclusion across anxious and avoidant attachment scores and discussed different ways of maintaining social bonds.

headline: Does being in a relationship change the link between brain structure and life satisfaction?
title: Together Means More Happiness: Relationship Status Moderates the Association between Brain Structure and Life Satisfaction
note: The researchers related MRI measurements and satisfaction ratings across relationship status, then examined how accounting for reported stress changed the relationship.

headline: Can expecting to be less hungry change the value that the brain assigns to food?
title: Mapping expectancy-based appetitive placebo effects onto the brain in women
note: The researchers used suggestions about appetite and modeled how food choices and prefrontal fMRI responses changed with hunger expectations.

headline: Does procrastination emerge from three distinct brain systems over two years?
title: The triple psychological and neural bases underlying procrastination: Evidence based on a two-year longitudinal study
note: The authors linked repeated procrastination measurements with imaging and psychological measures of self-control, emotion regulation and thinking ahead.

headline: Does putting a red stoplight on food packaging deter purchases by engaging frontal control?
title: Red for "Stop": "Traffic-Light" Nutrition Labels Decrease Unhealthy Food Choices by Increasing Activity and Connectivity in the Frontal Lobe
note: The authors compared traffic-light and numeric nutrition labels and interpreted activity and connectivity contrasts as a mechanism for healthier choices.

headline: Can a brain scan spot a punchline before a viewer finds it funny?
title: Decoding Humor Experiences from Brain Activity of People Viewing Comedy Movies
note: The authors aligned brain patterns with when viewers reported humor during comedies and interpreted advance decoding as evidence of a brief anticipatory state.

headline: Can brain signals recorded during resuscitation tell whether awareness returned?
title: AWAreness during REsuscitation - II: A multi-center study of consciousness and awareness in cardiac arrest
note: The researchers combined EEG monitoring with survivors’ reports in a multicenter cardiac-arrest study and interpreted some recorded patterns as possible markers of resumed cognition.

headline: Do the brainwaves that repeat most consistently tell which videos a wider audience prefers?
title: Spatiotemporal consistency of neural responses to repeatedly presented video stimuli accounts for population preferences
note: The authors compared repeat-view EEG across video stimuli and used the consistency of the patterns to estimate population preference.

headline: Does laughing at the same part of a film make viewers’ hippocampi synchronize?
title: Humor Appreciation Involves Parametric and Synchronized Activity in the Medial Prefrontal Cortex and Hippocampus
note: The authors related humor responses during viewing to activation and between-person similarity in hippocampal and medial prefrontal signals.

headline: Can a placebo make rejection hurt less through a pathway from frontal cortex to brainstem?
title: Frontal-Brainstem Pathways Mediating Placebo Effects on Social Rejection.
note: The authors combined a social rejection task, a placebo manipulation and fMRI and used brain–affect associations to identify a proposed pathway.

headline: Can a brain scan predict self-control in daily life by measuring how people value future consequences?
title: Predicting Real-Life Self-Control From Brain Activity Encoding the Value of Anticipated Future Outcomes.
note: The authors related fMRI measures of anticipated value to self-control on a laboratory task and to measures of everyday behavior.

headline: Does one serotonin-related gene variant track relationship satisfaction through a brain signal?
title: Genetic and neural correlates of romantic relationship satisfaction
note: The researchers compared genotype, neural activity and ratings of romantic relationship satisfaction using statistical mediation.

headline: Can brain signals help explain why people attribute bad character to someone with a facial anomaly?
title: Morality is in the eye of the beholder: the neurocognitive basis of the "anomalous-is-bad" stereotype
venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared evaluations and neural responses to faces with and without visible anomalies and interpreted patterns in terms of stereotypes.

headline: Can a brain scan explain why some people avoid taking responsibility for a group?
title: Computational and neurobiological foundations of leadership decisions.
note: The authors modeled choices about deciding for a group and related the fitted components to neural measures and external leadership scores.

headline: Do abstract paintings hold an artist’s attention while everyone else tunes out?
title: Art expertise modulates the emotional response to modern art, especially abstract: an ERP investigation
note: The authors compared late EEG responses from artists and nonartists viewing modern art and interpreted their opposite responses to abstract works as differences in arousal and sustained attention.

headline: Can an electric current make pictures less beautiful without making them uglier?
title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation over the Medial Prefrontal Cortex and Left Primary Motor Cortex (mPFC-lPMC) Affects Subjective Beauty but Not Ugliness
note: Participants rated images under different stimulation conditions. The authors used differential effects on beauty and ugliness ratings to argue that they are distinct dimensions.

headline: Does getting a joke feel like solving a puzzle to your brain?
title: Getting the Joke: Insight during Humor Comprehension - Evidence from an fMRI Study
note: The authors compared fMRI responses during humor comprehension and used overlaps with areas attributed to insight to infer a moment of realization.

headline: Can an ultra-high-field scanner catch an aha moment?
title: Ultra‐high‐field fMRI insights on insight: Neural correlates of the Aha!‐moment
note: The authors scanned people solving word problems and compared patterns for solutions reported with and without insight.

headline: Does making a face more symmetrical increase its beauty in the brain?
title: From physical symmetry to aesthetic value: investigating symmetry-induced attractiveness enhancement with fMRI.
note: The researchers altered visual symmetry, compared attractiveness ratings and mapped corresponding fMRI contrasts.

headline: Can the same comedy scene reveal a shared brain network for finding it funny?
title: Multivariate Identification of Functional Neural Networks Underpinning Humorous Movie Viewing
note: The researchers related fluctuations in viewers’ humor experience to a multivariate pattern of fMRI activity during a comedy.

headline: Does the intensity of a mystical experience show up in gray-matter volume?
title: The relationship between individual differences in gray matter volume and religiosity and mystical experiences: A preregistered voxel‐based morphometry study
note: This preregistered analysis compared regional volumes with religiosity and mystical-experience scores and reported no convincing structural evidence for the proposed relationships.

headline: Do meditating on kindness and focusing on attention change EEG in different ways?
title: Distinct Neural Activity Associated with Focused-Attention Meditation and Loving-Kindness Meditation
note: The authors compared task-related electrophysiology for practitioners of two meditation styles and used the differences to discuss sustained attention and responses to emotion.

headline: Does a green label make your brain less conflicted about buying something?
title: Environmental-friendly Eco-labeling Matters: Evidences From an ERPs Study
note: The authors varied eco-labels and interpreted shifts in purchase intentions and decision-related ERP components as reduced conflict and more positive emotion.

headline: Does the orbitofrontal cortex put a price on an everyday snack?
title: Orbitofrontal Cortex Encodes Willingness to Pay in Everyday Economic Transactions
note: Participants bid on foods while being scanned. The authors related fMRI activity to the amounts participants were willing to pay.

headline: Can a viewer’s brainwaves tell whether a short film gets a good rating?
title: EEG and peripheral markers of viewer ratings: a study of short films
note: The researchers related EEG and peripheral physiological measures recorded during short films to viewers’ ratings.

headline: Does a bitter aftertaste make food pictures look different to people prone to disgust?
title: The processing of visual food cues during bitter aftertaste perception in females with high vs. low disgust propensity: an fMRI study
note: The researchers compared neural responses to food cues during a bitter aftertaste among women with high and low disgust propensity.

headline: Can knowing where you sit in a social network tell how your brain will react to a health pitch?
title: Social Networks and Neural Receptivity to Persuasive Health Messages
note: The researchers linked features of participants’ social networks to activation while they viewed persuasive health messages.

headline: Can brain networks tell who will follow health advice after hearing it?
title: Brain System Integration and Message Consistent Health Behavior Change
note: The authors related network integration during health messages to later behavior consistent with those messages.

headline: Can an EEG trace separate fairness from selfishness in two money games?
title: Electrophysiological Markers of Fairness and Selfishness Revealed by a Combination of Dictator and Ultimatum Games
note: The authors related ERP responses across dictator and ultimatum games to fair and unfair offers and to groups defined by their choices.

headline: Does an unfair offer light up different areas if you think the other player had a choice?
title: Unfair? It depends: Neural correlates of fairness in social context
note: The authors varied the alternatives available to the proposer and treated differences in brain activity as evidence about the role of inferred intent in fairness.

headline: Does imagining a better past recruit more brain areas than remembering what happened?
title: Counterfactual thinking: an fMRI study on changing the past for a better future
note: The authors compared mental revisions of past events with recollection and interpreted additional activation in relation to episodic memory and mentalizing.

headline: Do anxious people’s memories change differently when they imagine what could have gone better?
title: Counterfactual thinking induces different neural patterns of memory modification in anxious individuals
note: The researchers compared fMRI pattern similarity before and after imagining alternative outcomes and examined whether it varied with trait anxiety.

headline: Does someone else’s regret show up in the same places as your own?
title: Understanding Others' Regret: A fMRI Study
note: The authors compared brain responses associated with understanding another person’s regret with regions implicated in experiencing regret oneself.

headline: Does a dishonest choice separately weigh your gain and someone else’s harm in the brain?
title: Contribution of self- and other-regarding motives to (dis)honesty
note: The authors fit a decision model with distinct self-gain and other-harm terms and related them to brain responses during honesty decisions.

headline: Does seeing a vulnerable person in need prime the motor system to help?
title: Altruistic responses to the most vulnerable involve sensorimotor processes
note: The authors related responses in a helping experiment to sensorimotor measures and used a separate motor task to examine the interpretation.

headline: Does the brain use one route for generous people and another for generous situations?
title: A unified neural account of contextual and individual differences in altruism
note: The researchers modeled evidence accumulation in altruistic choices and compared neural estimates linked to person-level and situation-level differences.

headline: Does being overpaid annoy a different brain system than being underpaid?
title: Neural responses to advantageous and disadvantageous inequity
note: The authors compared activity under advantageous and disadvantageous inequality and interpreted the differences in relation to status concerns.

headline: Can Granger analysis reveal which punishment region talks first?
title: Effective connectivity of brain regions underlying third-party punishment: Functional MRI and Granger causality evidence
note: The authors estimated directional relationships among fMRI time series while outsiders decided whether to punish unfairness.

headline: Does judging hurt feelings use different brain regions from judging a broken arm?
title: Neural substrates for moral judgments of psychological versus physical harm
note: Participants assessed scenarios involving psychological and physical harm. The authors compared fMRI responses across harm types.

headline: Can the brain combine a moral dilemma’s emotional cost with its utilitarian payoff?
title: Emotional and Utilitarian Appraisals of Moral Dilemmas Are Encoded in Separate Areas and Integrated in Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex
note: The experiment asked participants to evaluate dilemmas on different dimensions and used fMRI contrasts to infer component appraisals and their integration.

headline: Can inconsistencies in moral judgments be traced to how completely a prefrontal region represents the task?
title: Moral inconsistency is based on the vmPFC's insufficient representation across tasks and connectedness
note: The authors compared moral responses across tasks and used neural representation and connectivity measures to model consistency.

headline: Does a person’s competence at judging moral dilemmas show up at rest?
title: Moral competence and brain connectivity: a resting-state fMRI study
note: The authors related resting fMRI connectivity to a task-derived measure of moral competence.

headline: Does watching friends win feel like watching enemies lose to the brain?
title: I feel good whether my friends win or my foes lose: Brain mechanisms underlying feeling similarity
note: The authors compared neural patterns for favorable outcomes involving liked people and unfavorable outcomes involving disliked people.

headline: Does the same prefrontal region form your impression of me and guess my impression of you?
title: The role of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in automatic formation of impression and reflected impression
note: The authors related activity during impression formation and reflected-impression judgments to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex.

headline: Does knowing people from another racial group reduce a neural measure of empathy bias?
title: Intergroup relationships do not reduce racial bias in empathic neural responses to pain
note: The study compared pain-related responses across groups and examined whether intergroup relationships changed the measured bias.

headline: Can a different mindset reduce the brain’s in-group advantage for pain?
title: Manipulations of cognitive strategies and intergroup relationships reduce the racial bias in empathic neural responses.
note: The researchers manipulated the way participants viewed people from different groups and measured changes in neural responses to others’ pain.

headline: Does rejection of your group produce a similar brain response to personal rejection?
title: When group grievances become personal: The neural correlates of group and personal rejection
note: The authors compared fMRI responses during personal and group rejection and used overlap to discuss why collective grievances can feel personal.

headline: Can learning someone else likes a song change its value in your brain?
title: How the Opinion of Others Affects Our Valuation of Objects
note: The authors compared neural valuation signals for music before or after exposure to other people’s preferences.

headline: Does hearing how other people rate something privately change its neural value?
title: Social influence modulates the neural computation of value.
note: The researchers related changes in ratings and valuation-region responses to exposure to other people’s opinions.

headline: Does the brain price the same effort differently when it helps someone else?
title: Distinct neural representations for prosocial and self-benefiting effort
