note: The authors compared choices about exerting effort for self or others and modeled how brain activity tracked effort costs.

headline: Can older adults’ generosity, income and brain anatomy together indicate unhealthy brain aging?
title: Brain macrostructure correlates of financial altruism in older adults without dementia.
note: The authors related allocations in a financial game to structural MRI and examined whether the association depended on income among older adults without dementia.

headline: Does knowing who is watching change the brain activity behind a donation?
title: Familiarity and Audience Effects on Giving: A Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study.
note: The study varied audience and familiarity, then modeled how neural activity tracked giving and its social context.

headline: Does putting a face to one victim make the reward system push people to give?
title: Neural underpinnings of the identifiable victim effect: affect shifts preferences for giving
note: The authors varied whether recipients were identifiable and related donation differences to arousal measures and reward-region activity.

headline: Does your brain show less compassion when it blames the victim?
title: Compassion, guilt and innocence: An fMRI study of responses to victims who are responsible for their fate.
note: The researchers varied whether a victim was responsible for their situation and used fMRI contrasts during appraisal to infer regulation of compassion.

headline: Do people invest more generously when their basolateral amygdala is damaged?
title: Generous economic investments after basolateral amygdala damage
note: The study compared choices in social investment tasks across lesion and control groups and contrasted generosity with ratings of trust and expected return.

headline: Can the so-called bonding hormone favor selfish choices in the brain?
title: Oxytocin Facilitates Self-Serving Rather Than Altruistic Tendencies in Competitive Social Interactions Via Orbitofrontal Cortex
note: The authors compared effects of oxytocin in competitive decisions and linked increased self-serving choices with frontal reward-related activity.

headline: Does your brain value someone’s generosity differently when they meant to be generous?
title: When giving is good: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex activation for others’ intentions
note: The researchers compared activity for giving outcomes reached with different intentions and interpreted ventromedial prefrontal responses as sensitivity to both.

headline: Does oxytocin help the brain cooperate only while cooperation pays?
title: A functional MRI study on how oxytocin affects decision making in social dilemmas: Cooperate as long as it pays off, aggress only when you think you can win
note: The authors gave oxytocin or placebo and compared behavior and fMRI during social dilemmas that varied incentives and cues about other players.

headline: Can serotonin change how the striatum reacts to unfairness and retaliation?
title: Serotonin Modulates Striatal Responses to Fairness and Retaliation in Humans
note: The study manipulated serotonin availability and compared striatal responses to unequal offers and punitive decisions directed at oneself or others.

headline: Do brainwaves tell when a self-driving car made the wrong moral choice?
title: Event-related potentials reveal incongruent behavior of autonomous vehicles in the moral machine dilemma
note: The authors presented autonomous-vehicle dilemmas and compared EEG responses when the vehicle’s choice matched or conflicted with participants’ judgments.

headline: Does the brain appraise your online avatar as it would a real person?
title: How the human brain goes virtual: distinct cortical regions of the person-processing network are involved in self-identification with virtual agents.
note: The researchers scanned gamers and nongamers while they judged traits of themselves, their avatars or other people and compared responses in person-processing regions.

headline: Do close friends show more similar brain signals as they empathize with each other?
title: Brains in sync, friends in empathy: interbrain neural mechanisms underlying the impact of interpersonal closeness on mutual empathy
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors related interpersonal closeness and measures of empathy to neural alignment in paired social tasks.

headline: Does experimentally increasing closeness make two brains synchronize?
title: Testing the causal relationship between interpersonal closeness and inter-brain synchrony
note: The authors experimentally varied interpersonal closeness and reported increased coupling during interaction without evidence that closeness itself drove the increase.

headline: Does a successful science student’s brain sync with the classroom differently from a successful humanities student’s?
title: Inter-brain coupling reflects disciplinary differences in real-world classroom learning
note: The authors compared classroom neural coupling across subject categories and related different reference groups’ signals to learning outcomes.

headline: Does a complex sense of self give leaders a brain signature of adaptability?
title: The psychological and neurological bases of leader self-complexity and effects on adaptive decision-making.
note: The authors examined brain measures alongside leaders’ self-concepts and compared both with ratings of adaptive decision making.

headline: Can the brain’s dopamine-related maps explain who comes up with unusual ideas?
title: Neural, genetic, and cognitive signatures of creativity
note: The authors linked divergent-thinking patterns to brain imaging, gene-expression estimates and maps of neurotransmitter systems.

headline: Can resting brain connectivity tell how well a person generates creative ideas?
title: Creativity and the default network: A functional connectivity analysis of the creative brain at rest
note: The authors related resting-state connectivity to divergent-thinking performance and interpreted the differences in terms of the default network.

headline: Does generating original ideas require spontaneous and controlled brain networks to work together?
title: Default and Executive Network Coupling Supports Creative Idea Production
note: The researchers compared connectivity during an idea-generation task and related the coupling to creative performance.

headline: Do brain differences seen in criminal offenders also track psychopathic traits outside prison?
title: Brain Basis of Psychopathy in Criminal Offenders and General Population
note: The authors compared brain anatomy and responses to violence across forensic and community samples and related them to psychopathy measures.

headline: Does being more mindful change which networks stay connected at rest?
title: Trait Mindfulness and Functional Connectivity in Cognitive and Attentional Resting State Networks
note: The researchers compared questionnaire-rated trait mindfulness with functional connectivity in attention and cognitive networks.

headline: Do teenagers who play more video games have thicker frontal cortex?
title: Positive association of video game playing with left frontal cortical thickness in adolescents.
note: The authors related reported gaming time to structural MRI measures in adolescents and identified differences in left frontal regions.

headline: Does time on social media show up in early adolescents’ cortical anatomy?
title: Social media use and early adolescent brain structure: Findings from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study.
note: The authors compared reported social media use with brain structure in an adolescent population study.

headline: Can a resting connectome produce a temperament score?
title: Connectome-based individualized prediction of temperament trait scores.
note: The authors predicted questionnaire-based temperament measures from whole-brain functional connectivity.

headline: Can the distribution of gray matter tell which of the Big Five traits you score high on?
title: The Big Five of Personality and structural imaging revisited: a VBM - DARTEL study
note: The authors used voxel-based morphometry to compare regional brain volumes with Big Five scores.

headline: Does personality predict which brain regions lose volume faster over time?
title: A longitudinal study of the relationship between personality traits and the annual rate of volume changes in regional gray matter in healthy adults
note: The authors related personality traits to annualized regional gray-matter volume changes from repeated MRI.

headline: Do vascular and mental health measures explain why neuroticism tracks brain structure?
title: Association between neuroticism and brain-wide structural outcomes: Mediation by vascular and mental conditions
note: The authors related neuroticism to brain-wide structural measures and estimated mediation by vascular and mental conditions.

headline: Do structural brain measurements support personality neuroscience’s predictions about the Big Five?
title: Testing Predictions From Personality Neuroscience: Brain Structure and the Big Five
note: The authors tested hypotheses linking structural features with Big Five traits and reported which predictions the data supported.

headline: Can a compliment about your character change a brain signal tied to self-esteem?
title: Brain regions in response to character feedback associated with the state self-esteem
note: The researchers compared brain responses to positive and negative character feedback and related them to momentary self-esteem.

headline: Do compliments bounce off while criticisms sink in differently depending on self-esteem?
title: When compliments do not hit but critiques do: an fMRI study into self-esteem and self-knowledge in processing social feedback.
note: The authors compared responses to social feedback with how well it matched a person’s self-beliefs and with self-esteem.

headline: Can a brain response to someone else’s body reveal dissatisfaction with your own?
title: Neural correlates of appearance-based social comparison: The modulating effects of body dissatisfaction and person perspective.
note: The study related fMRI during appearance comparisons to body dissatisfaction and the perspective participants were asked to take.

headline: Does low self-esteem change which social feedback stands out in the brain?
title: Self-esteem modulates medial prefrontal cortical responses to evaluative social feedback.
note: The authors compared medial prefrontal responses to positive and negative evaluations and related the contrasts to individual self-esteem.

headline: Can an fMRI decoder recognize a color that a letter makes you see?
title: Multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI data for imaginary and real colours in grapheme-colour synaesthesia.
note: The authors compared patterns evoked by physical and synesthetic colors and found no evidence for the predicted involvement of the cortical color network.

headline: Does seeing colors in letters come with brain differences comparable in magnitude to a clinical condition?
title: Synesthesia is linked to large and extensive differences in brain structure and function as determined by whole-brain biomarkers derived from the HCP (Human Connectome Project) cortical parcellation approach
note: The researchers compared whole-brain structure and connectivity in synesthetes and controls and put the scale of the group differences in a clinical context.

headline: Does an imagined letter-color reach the brain later than a real color?
title: Temporal dissociation of neural activity underlying synesthetic and perceptual colors
note: The authors decoded color information from time-resolved neural signals and interpreted differences in the timing for physical and synesthetic colors as evidence for different processing stages.

headline: Does imagining tomorrow’s events require borrowing familiar scenery from memory?
title: Neural substrates of envisioning the future
note: The researchers compared activity during imagined personal futures and past events and interpreted visual-spatial responses as reuse of familiar contexts.

headline: Does one part of the brain stitch separate imaginary scenes into a longer story?
title: From single scenes to extended scenarios: The role of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex in the construction of imagery-rich events
note: The authors compared responses to single scenes and extended simulations and inferred a role for prefrontal regions in assembling imagined events.

headline: Is the medial temporal lobe building a scene or sending you to the future?
title: Medial Temporal Lobe Contributions to Episodic Future Thinking: Scene Construction or Future Projection?
note: The authors related activation to how much participants reported imagining a scene and to how much they thought about the future, and observed stronger evidence for a relation to scene construction.

headline: Does imagining the far future make the brain assign emotion differently from imagining next week?
title: Neural correlates of envisioning emotional events in the near and far future
note: The researchers varied how far ahead imagined events were and contrasted responses across time horizons and emotional conditions.

headline: Does an unanswered question feel aversive to the brain until the answer arrives?
title: Neural mechanisms underlying the induction and relief of perceptual curiosity
note: The authors induced perceptual curiosity with obscured images, then examined the neural response to clearing them up and interpreted it as relief and reward.

headline: Does learning a trivia answer give the brain a reward for satisfying curiosity?
title: Curiosity Satisfaction Increases Event-related Potentials Sensitive to Reward.
note: The researchers related curiosity ratings and EEG responses to the delivery of answers and interpreted an ERP difference as reward-like processing.

headline: Does curiosity about a video improve learning through attention rather than reward circuitry?
title: Broad brain networks support curiosity-motivated incidental learning of naturalistic dynamic stimuli with and without monetary incentives
note: The authors varied curiosity and monetary incentives during incidental learning and linked fMRI associations to broader attention and uncertainty networks.

headline: Can a brainwave pattern before awakening tell whether someone will remember a dream?
title: Cortical activation patterns herald successful dream recall after NREM and REM sleep.
note: The researchers compared EEG before REM and non-REM awakenings followed by recall or no recall and inferred common features of successful dream reporting.

headline: Can being prompted to dream about a puzzle help you solve it the next day?
title: Creative problem-solving after experimentally provoking dreams of unsolved puzzles during REM sleep
note: The authors used cues during REM sleep to provoke dreams about unsolved puzzles and compared dream incorporation with later problem-solving performance.

headline: Can a tasty-food scan tell when someone will give in to temptation outside the lab?
title: Neural Predictors of Giving In To Temptation in Daily Life
note: The authors related task-evoked neural activity to reports of everyday cravings and episodes of giving in.

headline: How much would you pay to avoid needing self-control, and can fMRI tell?
title: Quantifying the subjective cost of self-control in humans
note: The authors estimated a subjective cost for exercising self-control and related the fitted values to brain activity.

headline: Does the brain guard against temptation by taking future choices off the table?
title: Restricting Temptations: Neural Mechanisms of Precommitment
note: The researchers compared neural responses when participants chose to restrict later access to tempting options and when they relied on resisting them.

headline: Can a brain response to food and a gene variant predict future weight gain?
title: Reward Region Responsivity Predicts Future Weight Gain and Moderating Effects of the TaqIA Allele
note: The authors compared reward-region responsivity with later body-mass change and estimated whether the association differed by TaqIA genotype.

headline: Can brain activity while managing a craving predict what someone will eat later?
title: Brain Activity Associated With Regulating Food Cravings Predicts Changes in Self-Reported Food Craving and Consumption Over Time
note: The researchers related fMRI during craving regulation to subsequent self-reports of cravings and food consumption.

headline: Does almost winning a slot machine produce an amplified striatal response in problem gamblers?
title: Amplified Striatal Responses to Near-Miss Outcomes in Pathological Gamblers
note: The authors compared fMRI near-miss and other outcomes in gambling groups and tested whether the signal changed with a dopamine manipulation.

headline: Does rejecting a false belief activate the same control area used to stop an action?
title: Evidence for Spinozan "Unbelieving" in the Right Inferior Prefrontal Cortex.
note: The authors compared neural responses during believing and unbelieving and interpreted right prefrontal activation as support for a version of Spinoza’s theory.

headline: Does following orders make the brain treat your own action like a passive movement?
title: Coercion Changes the Sense of Agency in the Human Brain.
note: The researchers compared voluntary and coerced actions using a measure of perceived action–outcome timing and EEG responses to outcomes. They interpreted the changes as reduced agency.

headline: Can a person’s sense of responsibility survive coercion in a brain scanner?
title: The obedient mind and the volitional brain: A neural basis for preserved sense of agency and sense of responsibility under coercion
note: The study compared activity and measures of agency and responsibility during freely chosen and coerced actions, relating between-person variation to social-cognition areas.

headline: Does breaking your own habit of cheating recruit a different control process than breaking your habit of honesty?
title: Different Neural Mechanisms Underlie Non-habitual Honesty and Non-habitual Cheating.
note: The authors grouped participants by usual behavior in a cheating task and interpreted differences in inferior frontal responses on atypical decisions.

headline: Does being rejected by a potential date recruit the same networks as being accepted?
title: Common neural responses to romantic rejection and acceptance in healthy adults
note: The authors compared brain responses to romantic acceptance and rejection and interpreted shared activity in terms of inferring a potential partner’s intentions.

headline: Can a brain scan distinguish monogamous from nonmonogamous men when they see romantic scenes?
title: Differences in Neural Response to Romantic Stimuli in Monogamous and Non-Monogamous Men.
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to romantic stimuli in the two groups and discussed the contrast alongside findings from vole models of affiliation.

headline: Does the prefrontal cortex work out how to respond to a dominant person?
title: Dominance and submission: the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and responses to status cues
note: The researchers compared neural responses to dominant and submissive cues and interpreted functional coupling as information retrieval for adaptive social behavior.

headline: Does getting to know someone from another generation change how your brains synchronize?
title: Social interactions between people of same and different generations shape longitudinal changes in interpersonal neural synchrony, loneliness, and social connection.
note: The authors followed pairs interacting over time and related estimated interbrain synchrony to loneliness and perceived closeness.

headline: Does being afraid of math show up in a child’s brain anatomy?
title: Neurostructural correlate of math anxiety in the brain of children
note: The authors related math anxiety to structural MRI measurements in children and discussed implications for school achievement and dyscalculia.

headline: Can gray matter predict grades after accounting for family background?
title: Examining gray matter structure associated with academic performance in a large sample of Chinese high school students.
note: The authors compared gray-matter measures with academic performance in Chinese high school students and modeled the contribution of general intelligence.

headline: Can left parietal white matter tell how well you will do on the PSAT math section?
title: Individual differences in left parietal white matter predict math scores on the Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test
note: The researchers related diffusion MRI measures of white matter to math scores on the Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test.

headline: Does your response to single-digit sums reveal high school math competence?
title: Why mental arithmetic counts: brain activation during single digit arithmetic predicts high school math scores
note: The authors compared brain activity during simple arithmetic with broader mathematics scores and linked the association to calculation fluency.

headline: Do reasoning ability and acquired knowledge leave different neural signatures in teens?
title: Neural correlates differ between crystallized and fluid intelligence in adolescents.
note: The authors linked imaging measures to tests of fluid and crystallized intelligence and compared the patterns with maps of neurotransmitter systems.

headline: Do the anatomical networks of higher-IQ teenagers grow more efficient with age?
title: Association between structural brain network efficiency and intelligence increases during adolescence
note: The authors compared graph measures from structural imaging with IQ at different ages and modeled shared genetic influences.

headline: Can genes explain why the link between cortical thickness and IQ shifts with age?
title: The Dynamic Associations Between Cortical Thickness and General Intelligence are Genetically Mediated.
note: The authors used developmental MRI and genetically informative comparisons to estimate how much of the age-dependent thickness–IQ covariance was attributable to shared genes.

headline: Can a resting brain scan predict general intelligence if no single network is essential?
title: A distributed brain network predicts general intelligence from resting-state human neuroimaging data
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The authors trained models on distributed resting-state connectivity and tested how prediction changed when portions of the connectome were omitted.

headline: Can you make people less impatient by making time feel different to the brain?
title: Altering subjective time perception leads to correlated changes in neural activity and delay discounting
note: The researchers manipulated subjective time perception and linked changes in brain activity with changes in fitted delay-discounting rates.

headline: Can a brain model connect childhood trauma to putting things off years later?
title: Early wounds, delayed consequences: Brain-behavior modeling reveals neural pathways linking childhood trauma to procrastination
note: The authors linked childhood adversity, procrastination scores and brain features in a model interpreted through self-control and emotion regulation.

headline: Does a task feel less effortful to the brain simply because you can do it later?
title: A neuro-computational account of procrastination behavior
note: The researchers modeled discounting of delayed effort and reward, compared the estimates with fMRI responses and used the asymmetry to explain procrastination.

headline: Does a perfectionist’s brain respond more strongly to making a mistake?
title: To err is (perfectly) human: behavioural and neural correlates of error processing and perfectionism.
note: The authors split perfectionism into different dimensions and compared them with performance-monitoring signals during a task that produced errors.

headline: Can a map of the resting brain tell whether you prioritize goals conscientiously?
title: The goal priority network as a neural substrate of Conscientiousness
note: The authors estimated functional connectivity in a proposed goal-priority network and related it to conscientiousness questionnaire scores.

headline: Can an EEG signal distinguish the perseverance side of grit from the interest side?
title: The neural correlates of grit: Frontal lobe activity in grit effort and interest.
note: The authors related frontal EEG asymmetry to effort and interest subscales of a grit questionnaire.

headline: Does the striatum keep grit and a growth mindset in different resting networks?
title: The matter of motivation: Striatal resting-state connectivity is dissociable between grit and growth mindset.
note: The researchers related distinct patterns of resting striatal connectivity to questionnaire scores for grit and growth mindset.

headline: Can gray matter explain the connection between shyness and extraversion?
title: Brain structure links extraversion to shyness in late adolescence.
note: The authors compared anatomical MRI, personality ratings and shyness in late adolescence and modeled a structural link between the two traits.

headline: Can slow fluctuations in a resting scan tell how happy your life is?
title: Neural correlates of the happy life: the amplitude of spontaneous low frequency fluctuations predicts subjective well-being
note: The authors related spontaneous fMRI fluctuation amplitudes to cognitive and emotional components of subjective well-being.

headline: Does one resting brain signal explain why better social support feels like a happier community?
title: The neural correlates of community subjective well-being and its relationship to social support.
note: The authors related social support and community well-being scores to spontaneous brain activity and estimated statistical mediation.

headline: Does resting frontal asymmetry capture having a meaningful life better than feeling good?
title: Making a life worth living: neural correlates of well-being
note: The authors linked resting prefrontal activity to questionnaire measures of meaning-oriented and pleasure-oriented well-being.

headline: Do the brain’s switching patterns predict subjective happiness?
title: Brain networks of happiness: dynamic functional connectivity among the default, cognitive and salience networks relates to subjective well-being.
note: The authors related time-varying connectivity across default, control and salience networks to well-being scores and compared the result across samples.

headline: Can the size of the insula tell how mindfully you describe your feelings?
title: The structure of mindful brain
note: The researchers related questionnaire facets of mindfulness to gray-matter measures, including associations for the describing facet in the insula and amygdala.

headline: Can prefrontal connectivity explain losing your sense of self under LSD?
title: The Role of the Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in Ego Dissolution and Emotional Arousal During the Psychedelic State.
note: The authors related multimodal brain measures to reported ego dissolution and emotional arousal, discussing the patterns in terms of thalamic gating.

headline: Does a person lose their sense of self when the salience network loses cohesion?
title: Finding the self by losing the self: Neural correlates of ego-dissolution under psilocybin
note: The researchers related reported ego dissolution after psilocybin to connectivity patterns and inferred candidate networks that support the experience of a self.

headline: Does LSD make music evoke vivid personal imagery by changing one brain connection?
title: LSD modulates music-induced imagery via changes in parahippocampal connectivity
note: The researchers linked psychedelic and music conditions, self-reported imagery and parahippocampal functional connectivity.

headline: Can fainting bring on a near-death experience with its own EEG signature?
title: EEG signature of near-death-like experiences during syncope-induced periods of unresponsiveness
note: The authors compared EEG dynamics by whether participants who experienced brief unresponsiveness reported a near-death-like experience.

headline: Do pet owners have healthier brains because they live with animals?
title: Pet ownership is associated with greater cognitive and brain health in a cross-sectional sample across the adult lifespan
note: The researchers compared MRI and cognition across pet-ownership groups in a cross-sectional sample and discussed the associations as potentially protective.

headline: Can a dog’s brain distinguish a human’s fearful face from a sad one?
title: Dog brain representations of human facial expressions: Encoding happiness and differentiating specific negative expressions.
note: The authors used canine fMRI to classify responses to human faces with different emotional expressions and reported discrimination for some pairs of negative expressions.

headline: Does thinking a sweetener is sugar make the taste more rewarding to the brain?
title: Expectation Modulates Hedonic Experiences and Midbrain Responses to Sweet Flavor.
note: The authors manipulated beliefs about sweet flavor, then compared pleasantness ratings and midbrain responses to different sweeteners.

headline: Can a scan separate liking the smell of food from wanting to eat it?
title: Reward for food odors: an fMRI study of liking and wanting as a function of metabolic state and BMI
note: The authors compared neural responses to food odors with wanting and liking ratings across hunger states and body-mass measures.

headline: Does a front-of-package nutrition label change the features the brain uses to value food?
title: From attributes to value: Neural correlates of a front-of-package label on food decision-making - An fMRI study.
note: The researchers compared decisions and neural responses with and without nutrition labeling and modeled how attributes contributed to choice.

headline: Does an object gain value in your brain just because you imagine owning it?
title: The neural correlates of endowment effect without economic transaction.
note: The authors compared willingness to pay and accept in the absence of actual transactions and interpreted associated inferior frontal signals in terms of integrating value and loss aversion.

headline: Does telling teenagers a song is popular change the way their brains value it?
title: Neural mechanisms of the influence of popularity on adolescent ratings of music
note: The researchers showed adolescents music popularity information while collecting song ratings and fMRI data and examined activity as the ratings changed.

headline: Can a resting scan predict an online shopping addiction score?
title: Individualized prediction of online shopping addiction from whole-brain functional connectivity
note: The researchers modeled individual problematic-shopping scores from resting connectivity and interpreted the fitted networks in terms of impulsivity.

headline: Does favoring Beethoven or Eminem put the listening brain into a similar state?
title: Network science and the effects of music preference on functional brain connectivity: from Beethoven to Eminem
note: The authors compared connectivity while participants listened to preferred and less-preferred music and interpreted shared patterns in terms of personal preference across genres.

headline: Does nonsense humor recruit different areas from a joke whose punchline actually makes sense?
title: Neural substrates of incongruity-resolution and nonsense humor.
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to absurd and resolvable jokes and linked the responses to qualities such as sensation seeking.

headline: Does the brain work harder to suppress the stereotype that ugliness is bad than the idea that beauty is good?
title: Neural processing of the physical attractiveness stereotype: Ugliness is bad vs. beauty is good
note: The authors contrasted ERP responses during assignments of positive or negative attributes and interpreted group-level waveform differences as control of stereotype expression.

headline: Does a painting that moves you activate the network associated with thinking about yourself?
title: The brain on art: intense aesthetic experience activates the default mode network
note: The authors linked unusually high ratings of visual art to relative differences in default-network responses and inferred a role for personally relevant experience.

headline: Can a 40-minute walk in nature improve executive attention according to EEG?
title: Immersion in nature enhances neural indices of executive attention
note: The study compared attention-task behavior and electrical indices of executive control before and after nature or urban walks.

headline: Does a walk in nature quiet a brain region linked to dwelling on negative thoughts?
title: Nature experience reduces rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activation
note: The researchers compared rumination ratings and subgenual prefrontal perfusion after natural or urban walks and reported reductions in the nature condition.

headline: Does reading about the supernatural make the brain simulate an impossible event?
title: Unveiling the neural mechanisms of supernatural fiction comprehension using fNIRS.
note: The authors measured fNIRS during supernatural narratives and interpreted activity in a social-cognition network as evidence for simulation.

headline: Does getting lost in a story have a universal connectivity pattern?
title: Functional Brain Connectivity During Narrative Processing Relates to Transportation and Story Influence
note: The researchers related connectivity during narratives to immersion and influence measures and found limited consistency across stories.

headline: Does the brain hear a fictional character’s voice when you read in silence?
title: Processing Speech and Thoughts during Silent Reading: Direct Reference Effects for Speech by Fictional Characters in Voice-Selective Auditory Cortex and a Theory-of-Mind Network.
note: The researchers contrasted passages presenting speech or thought in different forms and mapped differences to voice-sensitive cortex and regions used in mentalizing tasks.

headline: Do trained dancers’ brainwaves align more closely as they watch a performance?
title: Dance on cortex: enhanced theta synchrony in experts when watching a dance piece
note: The authors compared theta synchronization during dance viewing across groups and interpreted stronger synchronization in dancers as more than motor observation alone.

headline: Does scientific or artistic achievement show up as a thinner cortex?
title: Neuroanatomy of creative achievement.
note: The study related cortical thickness to measures of creative achievement and interpreted regional associations in relation to control and default networks.

headline: Does a jazz improviser reach creative flow by letting go of cognitive control?
title: Creative flow as optimized processing: Evidence from brain oscillations during jazz improvisations by expert and non-expert musicians.
note: The authors compared EEG during rated improvisations across performers of different expertise and interpreted patterns during flow as learned processing with less control.

headline: Do more empathetic people’s brains hear sadness in music differently?
title: Trait Empathy Shapes Neural Responses Toward Sad Music
note: The authors compared neural responses to sad music across trait empathy scores and discussed whether the response reflects social emotion processing.

headline: Does being the kind of person who identifies with fictional characters show up in brain anatomy?
title: Identifying with fictive characters: structural brain correlates of the personality trait 'fantasy'.
note: The authors related a questionnaire’s fantasy subscale to structural MRI and discussed regional differences in light of character identification.

headline: Does the brain automatically assign a value to your favorite color?
title: The processing of color preference in the brain
note: The authors compared brain responses to colors with preference ratings and interpreted posterior midline activity as implicit valuation.

headline: Can a scan help predict who develops problematic short-video use because they fear missing out?
title: Neural, psychological, and transcriptomic predictors of short video addiction: A multi-site longitudinal study of fear of missing out and negative affect.
note: The authors combined behavioral ratings, MRI and transcriptomic maps to model separate pathways linking fear of missing out and negative affect to problematic use.

headline: Can brain structure, connectivity and gene-expression maps explain short-video addiction scores?
title: Neuroanatomical and functional substrates of the short video addiction and its association with brain transcriptomic and cellular architecture
note: The researchers related symptoms in a nonclinical sample to multimodal imaging and compared the spatial pattern with cellular and transcriptomic maps.

headline: Does an Instagram like carry different weight in a teenager’s brain than in a young adult’s?
title: Peer Influence Via Instagram: Effects on Brain and Behavior in Adolescence and Young Adulthood
note: The researchers varied apparent peer endorsement of photos and compared choices and fMRI responses across development.

headline: Does a brain form an opinion about beauty before it infers trustworthiness?
title: Neural time course and brain sources of facial attractiveness vs. trustworthiness judgment
note: The authors compared the time course and inferred sources of EEG responses during attractiveness and trustworthiness judgments.

headline: Does the brain divide social judgments of faces into separate modules?
title: The modular neuroarchitecture of social judgments on faces
note: The authors contrasted fMRI activity across judgments varying in social, emotional and face-specific content and interpreted dissociations as modularity.

headline: Can what you believe about a face change an early electrical signal of attractiveness?
title: Beauty is in the belief of the beholder: cognitive influences on the neural response to facial attractiveness
note: The investigators manipulated beliefs about faces and compared their effects with early face-evoked EEG activity.

headline: Does stopping a button press make the face on the screen less likable?
title: Response inhibition results in the emotional devaluation of faces: neural correlates as revealed by fMRI
note: The study paired faces with response inhibition, measured later evaluations and related changes in liking to activity during inhibition and evaluation.

headline: Does a scan represent trustworthiness and dominance as distances in the same space?
title: A Multidimensional Neural Representation of Face Impressions
note: The authors modeled similarities among people’s impressions of faces and compared those distances with patterns of activity during face evaluation.

headline: Can amygdala activity patterns estimate an implicit prejudice score?
title: Neural signals in amygdala predict implicit prejudice toward an ethnic outgroup.
note: The authors used multivariate fMRI analyses during face viewing and related them to performance on a measure of implicit bias toward an ethnic out-group.

headline: Does the amygdala’s response to an out-group face change depending on what you are trying to judge?
title: Controlling racial prejudice: social-cognitive goals affect amygdala and stereotype activation
note: The researchers varied the observer’s task and compared fMRI and lexical measures of stereotype activation across goals.

headline: Does a difference in amygdala response to racial groups emerge during adolescence?
title: Amygdala sensitivity to race is not present in childhood but emerges over adolescence
note: The authors compared face-evoked activity across age, then examined whether reported peer diversity went with a smaller contrast.

headline: Do soccer fans recruit a particular region when they are willing to help fellow fans?
title: Neural bases of ingroup altruistic motivation in soccer fans
note: The researchers compared costly helping for in-group and other targets and interpreted fMRI differences in terms of in-group altruistic motivation.

headline: Can a cultural prime change the first brain responses to your own face or a friend’s?
title: Dynamic cultural modulation of neural responses to one's own and friend's faces
note: The researchers compared face-evoked EEG signals after cultural primes and interpreted the differences as rapid shifts in self-processing.

headline: Does a Chinese participant’s brain include their mother in the same region it uses for the self?
title: Neural basis of cultural influence on self-representation
note: The authors compared self and mother trait judgments in Chinese and Western participants and used differences in medial prefrontal responses to infer cultural variation in self-representation.

headline: Does a face become more memorable when it looks better than the brain expected?
title: Remembering unexpected beauty: Contributions of the ventral striatum to the processing of reward prediction errors regarding the facial attractiveness in face memory
note: The authors modeled prediction errors for facial attractiveness and related them to striatal activity, hippocampal coupling and memory.

headline: Does seeing a beautiful face have a different reward value from being willing to work to keep seeing it?
title: Beautiful faces have variable reward value: fMRI and behavioral evidence.
note: The researchers compared explicit attractiveness ratings, button presses that prolonged viewing and reward-related fMRI responses.

headline: Do anonymous organ donors recruit a brain system associated with mammalian parenting when they see someone in distress?
title: Amygdala-midbrain connectivity indicates a role for the mammalian parental care system in human altruism
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers compared amygdala–midbrain coupling in costly altruists and controls and interpreted group differences through parental care.

headline: Can the brain sense aggression from someone’s body odor?
title: Chemosensory danger detection in the human brain: Body odor communicating aggression modulates limbic system activation
note: The authors presented odors collected in different contexts and related differences in neural activity to threat and aggression processing.

headline: Does smelling someone’s stress sweat make an otherwise neutral face command more attention?
title: Second-hand stress: inhalation of stress sweat enhances neural response to neutral faces.
note: The authors compared EEG responses to neutral faces after exposure to different sweat samples and interpreted changes as heightened attention.

headline: Does the brain handle the same advice differently when it comes from a person instead of a machine?
title: Advice Taking from Humans and Machines: An fMRI and Effective Connectivity Study
note: The authors varied who gave advice and compared choice behavior and estimated directional coupling between regions.

headline: Can brainwaves reveal how much you trust an algorithm after it makes a mistake?
title: Learning From the Slips of Others: Neural Correlates of Trust in Automated Agents
note: The authors measured EEG while people monitored automated performance and related error-related signals to reported trust.

headline: Does watching social movements in sync line up gamma waves in mothers and children?
title: Perception of social synchrony induces mother-child gamma coupling in the social brain
note: The authors measured simultaneous EEG in mother–child pairs and compared interbrain coupling across displays of social synchrony.

headline: Does a stressed parent’s brain synchronize less with their child’s?
title: Parenting Stress Undermines Mother-Child Brain-to-Brain Synchrony: A Hyperscanning Study
note: The authors measured fNIRS in mother–child pairs and related parenting-stress scores to brain-to-brain coupling during shared viewing.

headline: Can a scan distinguish generosity driven by guilt from generosity driven by shame?
title: Human neurocomputational mechanisms of guilt-driven and shame-driven altruistic behavior.
note: The researchers fit separate computational models for helping after guilt or shame and related the model terms to different activity patterns.

headline: Can a photo of your partner act as a painkiller by engaging reward circuitry?
title: Viewing pictures of a romantic partner reduces experimental pain: involvement of neural reward systems
note: The authors compared experimental pain while participants viewed a partner or comparison stimuli and related changes in pain ratings to reward-related activity.

headline: Is giving money away linked to happiness through prefrontal control of the brain’s reward system?
title: A neural link between generosity and happiness
note: The authors compared participants making different spending commitments and related generosity and happiness ratings to estimated coupling during a giving task.

headline: Can an apology change the brain response that goes with forgiving someone?
title: The strength of a remorseful heart: psychological and neural basis of how apology emolliates reactive aggression and promotes forgiveness
note: The authors compared responses to offenders who apologized or did not and linked electrophysiological and behavioral measures to forgiveness and retaliation.

headline: Can a brain scan distinguish deciding whether a headline is true from deciding whether to share it?
title: The neural basis of fake news accuracy judgments and sharing decisions
note: The authors compared neural responses during accuracy and sharing judgments of news and assessed how one judgment influenced the other.

headline: Does an fMRI pattern explain why misinformation keeps influencing people after a correction?
title: Keeping track of 'alternative facts': The neural correlates of processing misinformation corrections
note: The researchers compared responses during reasoning with corrected information and interpreted the patterns as concurrent retention of both versions.

headline: Does getting paid for one random trial make people look more risk-averse in behavior and EEG?
title: What you give is what you get: Payment of one randomly selected trial induces risk-aversion and decreases brain responses to monetary feedback.
note: The authors compared payment rules, measuring risky choices and electrical responses to monetary feedback.

headline: Does eating enough chocolate turn its brain reward into an aversion?
title: Changes in brain activity related to eating chocolate: from pleasure to aversion
note: The researchers repeatedly offered chocolate while measuring subjective responses and cerebral blood flow and interpreted different regional patterns at pleasure and satiety.

headline: Can the brain stop responding to chocolate before you notice your craving fade?
title: The craving stops before you feel it: neural correlates of chocolate craving during cue exposure with response prevention.
note: The authors compared cue-evoked reward activity and craving reports during exposure to chocolate cues and discussed whether neural changes preceded subjective change.

headline: Can the choices of two people in a trust game be predicted from EEG oscillations?
title: Hierarchical Neural Prediction of Interpersonal Trust
note: The researchers related beta-band activity around decision making to trial-level trust choices.

headline: Does culture change how the ventromedial prefrontal cortex represents lottery odds?
title: Culture-related differences in the neural processing of probability during mixed lottery value-based decision-making
note: The authors modeled responses to mixed lotteries across cultural groups and interpreted fMRI differences as variation in probability and value computation.

headline: Can the ventral striatum predict who will keep making expensive choice errors months later?
title: Fatal attraction: ventral striatum predicts costly choice errors in humans
note: The researchers related striatal activity during a choice task to costly errors and tested whether the association carried over to a later task.

headline: Does missing an opportunity light up the striatum and change what you choose next?
title: Ventral striatal signal changes represent missed opportunities and predict future choice.
note: The authors compared fMRI responses to missed opportunities and used striatal and insular signals to predict behavior on a subsequent round.

headline: Does an fMRI signal explain why a gambler thinks a losing streak is about to end?
title: An fMRI study of risk-taking following wins and losses: implications for the gambler's fallacy
note: The authors compared risk choices and brain responses after wins and losses and interpreted the patterns in terms of decision biases such as the gambler’s fallacy.

headline: Does a moral dilemma use different brain circuitry when the choice actually costs you something?
title: Differential neural circuitry and self-interest in real vs hypothetical moral decisions
note: The authors compared real and hypothetical moral decisions and modeled how prefrontal activity related to self-interested choices.

headline: Does blaming someone recruit different regions depending on how independent you see yourself?
title: Blame and Praise cross-culturally: An fMRI investigation into causal attribution and moral judgment
note: The researchers related fMRI activity to situational and personal attributions while participants apportioned blame or praise, and compared the associations by self-construal.

headline: Does imagining yourself as the agent of a moral act use a network for thinking about yourself?
title: The self as a moral agent: linking the neural bases of social agency and moral sensitivity
note: The researchers compared fMRI responses while participants imagined socially neutral or emotionally charged conduct and interpreted overlaps with default and moral-sensitivity regions.

headline: Does the brain evaluate a morally tainted profit differently if it goes to charity?
title: Neurocomputational mechanisms underlying immoral decisions benefiting self or others
note: The authors compared decisions about earning money through a morally objectionable act for oneself or for a charity and related the fitted decision variables to fMRI responses.

headline: Does a rival team’s failure activate the same reward system as your team’s success?
title: Us versus them: social identity shapes neural responses to intergroup competition and harm
note: The authors scanned sports fans watching game outcomes and related ventral striatal activity to reported pleasure and willingness to harm a rival fan.

headline: Does playing a violent video game dull the brain’s response to someone else’s pain?
title: Neuroimaging and behavioral evidence that violent video games exert no negative effect on human empathy for pain and emotional reactivity to violence
note: The researchers assigned participants to play under controlled gaming conditions and found no evidence of reduced empathy in the neural or behavioral measures they used.

headline: Does decoding someone’s intended action decode an intention or just the scene they picture?
title: Decoding intentions of self and others from fMRI activity patterns
note: The authors compared fMRI patterns when participants considered their own or others’ intentions and found the information could be explained by visuospatial features shared with imagining action outcomes.

headline: Does a hangover blunt the brain’s electrical response to a reward?
title: Alcohol hangover impacts learning and reward processing within the medial-frontal cortex.
note: The researchers compared task performance and EEG responses to feedback in hangover and comparison conditions and interpreted the changes as altered reward-based learning.

headline: Can trying hard to suppress a thought about chocolate quiet the brain systems tied to cravings?
title: Suppressing images of desire: Neural correlates of chocolate-related thoughts in high and low trait chocolate cravers.
note: The authors compared brain responses while people with different chocolate-craving scores suppressed or engaged with chocolate-related imagery.

headline: Does deciding to throw something away use different neural responses from deciding to acquire it?
title: The neural bases of acquisitiveness: decisions to acquire and discard everyday goods differ across frames, items, and individuals.
note: The authors varied whether participants framed a decision about goods as acquisition or disposal and interpreted activation patterns in relation to individual differences in acquisitiveness.

headline: Does a bad smell make a disgusted face easier for the brain to process?
title: Processing of disgusted faces is facilitated by odor primes: a functional MRI study
note: The researchers paired odor primes with facial expressions and examined how odor valence changed behavioral performance and emotion-related fMRI responses.
